item.title: Phantom Blade Zero First Impressions Review | Already Shaping Up to Be One of 2026’s Coolest Action Games
item.description: 2026.10.26 Phantom Blade Zero is a stylish action RPG that blends classic Chinese wuxia with steampunk-inspired machinery called “kungfupunk.” Learn more about the game’s plot, gameplay, and our first impressions of the game.
item.content:encoded:
Phantom Blade Zero is a stylish action RPG that blends classic Chinese wuxia with steampunk-inspired machinery called “kungfupunk.” Read on to learn more about the game’s plot, gameplay, and our first impressions of the game.
## Already Shaping Up to Be One of 2026’s Coolest Action Games
When S-Game announced Phantom Blade Zero during the PlayStation Showcase in May 2023, the world was already looking forward to the next wave of action RPGs that could rival FromSoftware’s acclaimed Elden Ring.
Phantom Blade Zero was no different. It was unveiled just three years after Game Science revealed its own attempt to claim a slice of the action RPG market with Black Myth: Wukong. Phantom Blade Zero had a kickass trailer that showed how well this budding studio could pull off both cinematic sequences and flashy gameplay. These games, alongside other Chinese-developed titles like Wuchang: Fallen Feathers and Where Winds Meet, share the same level of confidence you’d come to expect from the country’s game developers, packed with flashy action and a clear passion for Chinese lore and legends.
The question is: Does Phantom Blade Zero live up to the enormous hype surrounding its initial reveal? It’s not really something I can answer with a firm yes or no just yet. However, if it’s any consolation, during my time exploring its decrepit “kungfupunk” world, I’ve fallen more and more in love with its systems and gameplay, with plenty of moments that have left me genuinely astonished. That said, there are also moments when certain things feel too lenient or outright frustrating in its combat, especially during the first few hours.
While I can’t give a final verdict just yet, as I’m still about 15 hours through the game, I can confidently say that Phantom Blade Zero is one damn cool action RPG.
### Putting the Punk in Kung Fu
“Kungfupunk” is the marketing term S-Game keeps using to describe Phantom Blade Zero. It refers to a blend of classic Chinese wuxia storytelling, kung fu, and dynastic settings with the raw, brutalist architecture of steampunk, complete with heavy machinery and a whole lot of gears. Throughout the first few hours of the game, you’re greeted not just by metal and industrial music, but also by the sight of massive factories billowing with black smoke, where freaky experiments defy the very laws of nature, resulting in the chaos you’re about to deal with.
The story in Phantom Blade Zero is pretty straightforward, which genuinely surprised me, since games in this genre tend to revel in obtuse storytelling that requires a popular YouTuber to explain their lore. From the get-go, you know that you’re playing as Soul, a dead man walking who’s living on borrowed time, with only 66 days left to live. He must find the people responsible for the conspiracy that led to his death.
It’s that simple premise that keeps you invested in its world, as you’re also curious about who these people are and why they’re responsible for the downfall of Wulin, its dark-fantasy setting. There are a lot of names to keep track of, and players who’ve played any wuxia game know the struggle of remembering who’s who. Thankfully, the game does a great job of keeping your lore knowledge in check by highlighting key terms in yellow and providing an entire archive to explore if you want to dig deeper into its twisted rabbit hole.
But Soul isn’t doing all this adventuring alone. Along the way, he encounters an eclectic cast of characters, from pretty blacksmiths to grotesque monstrosities that make up some of the game’s fantastic boss battles that demand careful precision in its parry and dodge-based gameplay.
### Keep Those Parries Going in its Gameplay
If not for its twist on the kung fu genre, Phantom Blade Zero’s biggest draw would be its hyperkinetic gameplay, which offers the same kind of satisfaction as other “parryslop” titles like Sekiro and the new Onimusha. It wants you to pay attention to the glint of an enemy’s sword and react in time to deliver a powerful counterattack.
Not to mention, its selection of boss fights can rival even FromSoftware’s rogues’ gallery of enemies, as the variety of encounters ranges from standard sword-wielding warriors to a puppet-controlled former general from a bygone army.
Games like these exist purely to give you that dopamine rush of landing thirty sword strikes with perfect parries, accompanied by the clink and clang of metal with every hit. It’s one of the reasons people call it a pseudo-rhythm game, as you’re expected to listen for the right cues and mash that L1 button at just the right moment.
What S-Game has accomplished with Phantom Blade Zero is a level of surgical precision in combat that matches its peers. Perfect parries and dodges are your bread and butter when dealing with the many threats lurking in its world, while additional tools like Soul’s Phantom Edge abilities give him more options for dealing massive damage to enemies, albeit with limited uses.
One of my only complaints so far (now that I’ve made it past the game’s third map) is that its combat takes a while to get used to because everything moves really, really fast, making it difficult to tell what an enemy is going to do next. The moment boss fights begin, you’re bombarded with a flurry of sword slashes that force you to lock in and mash that L1 button. There are telegraphed moves that are easy to counter, but when things get too crazy, like during a super-powered second phase, you’ve barely got any options other than to pray that your button-mashing can save you. Things can get pretty chaotic, and the timing can feel awkward at times, especially when there’s so much happening on screen at once, from incoming projectiles to command grabs that come out of nowhere.
The good news is that these complaints are mostly tied to my first five hours or so with the game. The early bosses were incredibly difficult, and I’m sure there will be players complaining about that first “skill-check” Huntsman. I nearly screamed in frustration because Soul loves to perform a dramatic flip before striking an enemy, costing me precious frames. After that, however, things become a bit more manageable as I’ve unlocked and upgraded most of my favorite weapons, including a Drunken Swordmaster’s magical blade that lets you fling it around enemies from a distance while getting drunk on booze.
### It’s Not a Soulslike After All
One of the game’s biggest surprises, especially for someone like me who tried to avoid most of its marketing campaign, was discovering that Phantom Blade Zero isn’t a Soulslike. I’m pretty sure I’m not the only one who assumed the game would play like its inspirations, but what shocked me most was how simple everything is. Phantom Blade Zero takes a more casual approach, much like Black Myth: Wukong, which doesn’t overwhelm you with a massive open world or five layers of underground maps to explore.
Its gameplay is surprisingly straightforward: you move from one hallway to another, deal with enemies, find a chest tucked away along an off-the-beaten path, and eventually make your way to a big boss battle.
The difficulty options are available from the very beginning, allowing you to tailor the experience to your preferences. This is a level of accessibility I completely welcome, especially for players who want to play the game their own way instead of getting bodied by the first boss they encounter.
Another thing that impressed me was how resting at Bonfires, or Bells in this game, doesn’t respawn enemies. That means once you’ve cleared an entire encampment of mobs and died after falling into some random pit, you’ll return to the same spot without having to deal with those enemies again. You can then pilfer all the treasures without distractions.
Eliminating respawning enemies is an interesting change for an action game, as it prevents players from cheesing bosses too easily by farming respawning enemies. However, it’s also a double-edged sword, since you can’t easily find other ways to gather upgrade materials or improve your gear when the next part of the map is locked behind a main boss. Instead, you’re encouraged to head straight for the game’s objectives to collect those nifty upgrade materials.
Even bosses aren’t safe from the game’s more casual approach to accessibility. Once you’ve cleared a boss’s first phase but died during the second, the game lets you jump straight into the second phase on your next attempt. This saves you precious time that you can spend learning the boss’s newly acquired moves, while also replenishing your healing flasks and Phantom Edge uses.
If limited resources and upgrades are your concern, however, it’s not that big of a deal, as the game offers free respeccing at no extra cost. The only exception is when you’ve upgraded certain weapons to Level 10 or higher, as you’ll need a specific item to respec them. Everything else is pretty lenient, so if you don’t like a new weapon you unlock after a boss fight, you can always head to the local blacksmith or a bonfire to revert your choices and find the one that suits you best.
### More Things to Do in The World
Even after 15 or so hours exploring the world of Phantom Blade Zero, I know there’s still so much more left for me to do because the game keeps opening up and giving me plenty of side activities and secret bosses to tackle.
These extra bosses are incredibly challenging as well, and I wouldn’t recommend taking them on too early, as you’ll likely find yourself in a battle of attrition due to their massive health pools. These are best saved for the late game, when Soul is beefier than ever, equipped with the best upgrades and the right Phantom Edge tools.
One more thing I almost forgot to mention is how Phantom Blade Zero incorporates light Metroidvania elements into its exploration, where you can’t progress through certain areas without a specific ability or Phantom Edge. Whether it’s a grappling hook to reach otherwise inaccessible surfaces or a massive axe to break down a wall, these tools help you explore more of the world organically. You only unlock these abilities after defeating certain key bosses throughout the realm, giving you more reasons to revisit previously explored areas.
There’s also Soul’s 66-day time limit, though I’m still not entirely sure how much it affects the game beyond its story. So far, it doesn’t seem to work like The Blood of Dawnwalker’s timer, where taking on quests shaves precious hours off your remaining time. From what I can tell, the countdown only advances when you rest at certain bonfires, and it hasn’t felt particularly restrictive to my journey yet. If you want to make good use of this system, there’s also a Permadeath mode you can unlock after finishing the game, which gives you only 66 lives before you have to start from scratch.
There’s already plenty of depth to Phantom Blade Zero’s action RPG adventure, and the game keeps getting better every time I enter a new area. My only issues so far are how tanky the bosses can be and how difficult the early game feels. Beyond that, the game has so much swagger that I’m already excited to see what boss fights await me around the next corner and how its 66-day time limit affects the story.
If I had to give it a temporary rating before rolling credits, I’d give Phantom Blade Zero a strong 8 out of 10, assuming its momentum doesn’t fizzle out in the later stages.

item.title: Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave DLC Has Four More Routes, And I Think I Know How They’ll Play Out
item.description: 2026.10.26 Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave just revealed that we’re getting the routes for the other four Flame Lords next year, and I might be able to predict how they’re supposed to work in both gameplay and narrative terms.
item.content:encoded:
Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave just revealed that we’re getting the routes for the other four Flame Lords next year, and I might be able to predict how they’re supposed to work in both gameplay and narrative terms.
## Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave DLC Reveals More Routes to Expand Its Narrative
### One of Nintendo’s Worst Kept Secrets
In my review of Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, I detailed some of the biggest problems that the game had in the latter acts of its narrative—plot threads that vanish, details that get dropped, or, most annoyingly, a lot of setups that eventually go unexplained. On the same topic, this made for the low-hanging fruit that many players know now: it was obvious, even before the recent announcement, that the four other Flame Lords—Bertrand, Talimund, Anatolia, and Orchel—would eventually have their own routes.
While Intelligence Systems did mention that their routes were cut in their AMA back in September 15, 2026, they're no stranger to adding DLC to add more context and depth to their narratives. There are many examples of this in their previous installments, but let’s go with one of the least spoiler-y plot threads that actually happens in Fortune's Weave’s first two hours: Bertrand’s introductory cutscene in the Heroic Games.
In this scene, he gets introduced as a living legend in the Arena to fight in a special exhibition match to start the tournament off. But he loses to this mysterious character, one that’s never seen again after this one match. Given the context of how he develops, it’s one of those things that players know should lead up to something, which is why it was obvious that he was going to get his very own route eventually.
There are many more examples of this, but believe me when I say that the four other Flame Lords getting their own routes was just a matter of time. And I think I have a good enough guess on how each of them is going to play out.
Before anything else, keep in mind that these are merely speculations about how each DLC route will work, using inferences drawn from the game's many, many interactions and cutscenes. I could be completely wrong about these predictions. Hell, their routes might not even have a Part 1 as the main four do, but isn’t that part of the fun when looking forward to new content?
Warning: Sections of this article contain heavy spoilers about the various main characters of Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave.
## Bertrand—The White-Maned Demon
### Reminiscent of the Older Fire Emblem Gameplay Loop
Let’s start with the White-Maned Demon, which is probably the easiest route to cover and the one I’m looking forward to the most. Narratively, there’s a lot to unpack about his involvement in the story. His route will most likely answer how the Cydonia Massacre came to be and how he was accused of regicide right after. More importantly, it will answer two key questions: the identities of Gilchris and Aswan, and his relationship with both. We know these two characters are pivotal to the Kingdom of Arago, but we don’t exactly know who they really are and why they’re so attached to Bertrand, especially the former.
Then, there’s the matter of his appearance, specifically how it changes after his undocumented fight with Orchel’s team in the Heroic Games. We know from Cai’s route that Aswan gives him the Bloodaxe, which turns into the Zalmoxis (the very same axe that Sothis used to execute Balor) after he goes "all red" during his fight against Orchel. Beyond the obvious fact that Orchel cleanses him of that corruption, we might gain some insight into how the weapon became corrupted in the first place.
There’s also the matter of his freedom, AKA the completion of the Trial of the Chariot, and how he becomes the King of Brezarant in Act 2. We don’t learn whether he gets a wish, since he’s forced to fight under Mars’ name as part of the Trial of the Chariot, but we do know that he eventually earns his freedom upon completing his sentence. This could be where Mars reveals his master plan of using the Trial to test whether he is capable of becoming the next king of Brezarant. As a result, we might finally know who the hell Cruaidin is, especially since he might be one of the agents tasked with testing Bertrand under Mars’ orders.
As for his gameplay, Bertrand is in prison for the entirety of the Heroic Games, meaning he probably won’t have much Free Time to spare. In fact, I think his route will appeal to most classic Fire Emblem fans, since it will likely resemble an older game without all the fluff that the new games have really come to embrace.
His route will likely be similar to Act 2’s gameplay loop, where players have a few options for spending their Free Time—develop his army’s Skill Proficiencies, ask them to train for EXP, or spend time to level up a specific temple for his Divine Blessing mechanic—all from the comfort of his cell.
The more interesting thing to think about is how he’ll end up recruiting other units or even how he’s supposed to level up his Supports, since he doesn’t have the opportunity to either talk to others personally or go for a meal at the inn. While I’m not as confident in this part as I am in my prediction of his core gameplay loop, I would really appreciate it if his recruitment were reminiscent of the older games, where he has to talk to potential recruits during battle and convert them to his side afterward.
## Talimun—The Swashbuckling King
### The Wild Card With More Than Meets the Eye
Next we’ll move on to the richest man in all of Dagda, Talimun, also known as the owner of the Vandahl Trading Company.
When it comes to his narrative, he is one of the most interesting characters to learn about and draw inferences from, specifically because he’s a demigod. In his many Supports and other cutscenes, we know that he’s been around for a while. So much so that he knows some of the different ancestors that the other characters have personally. On that end, he’s a character with much to reveal about his lineage and ties to the Order of Mithras.
There’s also the matter of his motive. He reveals that his wish is to buy the land of Dagda, which seems absurd at first glance. Given the context of knowing Solel, however, he might just end up selling it to him. But there is a strong possibility that he might not even win the tournament in his own route. This pertains to the timing of when he ends up fighting and defeating Maria, which he reveals in an exclusive cutscene with Lind in Act 2 if you don’t accomplish his Paralogue.
In the same scene, Talimund reveals his family history, specifically that he’s the son of the pirate Vandahl and the same Maria that he just off-screened. The latter of whom is known as one of Balor's daughters and an orchestrator of the Cydonia Massacre. Based on the ending of Leda’s route and the aforementioned scene with Lind, it probably occurred right after the conclusion of the Heroic Games, which might be the final battle to wrap up his route.
This means his route will probably end up in a similar situation to Theodora's, where he bows out of the competition early and goes off to resolve his own matters outside Dagsion.
On the gameplay side, I think it would be great if his route were the easiest way to build up Renown, or if he immediately started at a high, or even max, level without doing any sidequests. After all, he is supposed to be the most well-known out of all the Flame Lords because of his ownership of the Vandahl Trading Company. Consequently, with a high Renown, he should be able to recruit more units to his cause much more quickly than the other Flame Lords.
Speaking of which, to make his sidequests more distinctive than the rest of the cast, his quests will probably involve either bartering for specific rewards or requiring a set amount of gold to deal with his clients. Similarly, his map gimmick would be the ability to assign procurement and organize orders with his many merchants, and to collect weekly rewards from his main office at the port of Dagsion.
## Anatolia—Queen of the Erased
### Hints About the Sothisverse and Civilization Before the Great Undoing
As mysterious as her moniker "Mystery Bride," Anatolia’s route is the one we know the least about. We know her as a Mediator who was made to protect Kunlun or The Forbidden Land, and not much else. In Hannibal, one of the Grand Megaliths or crashed spaceships that you find while exploring the world, there’s an odd transmission made by another mysterious character named Orpheus who reveals that they are waiting for her to arrive in the faraway land of Solomon, which is only reachable by sea.
On Theodora’s route, we learn that she leaves Dagsion to travel to the same land, where the player can choose whether to lend her Saramis’ flagship or not. Assuming that she does get to Solomon using Theodora’s ship, this will probably take place around her 9th or 10th chapter, in between the Heroic Games.
Given the context of Anatolia’s Paralogue, the Odd Transmission, and how she mentions that her people relocated to the East in the latter acts, it’s safe to assume they found something in Solomon to help them rebuild their society, one where they can find a permanent place to call home. At the same time, this part of her story will reveal how Long meets his demise, which we know occurs during her journey to Solomon.
There’s not enough information about the People of the White Egg in the current game other than that they’re survivors of the Great Undoing. It’ll be interesting to see how they’ll detail that she and her cohorts (Sha Lan, Nezha, and Dadao) are synthetic human beings, given that all three are Mediators tasked with protecting Kunlun. We might also see a completely different side of Anatolia, especially since there’s a very subtle shift in her character from when players first meet her to her last interaction with Fabio and Dietrich.
Her route should also answer her connections to Eshmel. While Mediators may not be cut from the same cloth, her ties to Zenon might reveal more about the creation of Mediators, Heart Cores, and more. There might also be more information about the weaponry and martial arts the People of the White Egg use and practice, especially since these are a big part of their identity.
It’ll be interesting to see how her route will play out. Based on the information we have in the current routes, Anatolia might win the Heroic Games by default, similar to Dietrich, since Theodora bows out of the tournament early. It’s unclear whether she’ll unlock the gates of Kunlun, especially since she does everything in her power to relocate them to the East in her Paralogue. But it’s also easy to assume that she’ll get a very different ending from what we expect, maybe a special meeting with Troy to finally compare notes, perhaps?
From a gameplay perspective, she’ll most likely have some sort of Renown and Support-building aspect tied to her fortune-telling, which seems to be an exclusive mechanic for her that players can currently interact with in the game. This could mean that her route will give her the chance to interact with many of the game's characters, as well as give us a clearer idea of how she conducts these fortune-telling sessions en masse.
Additionally, her sidequests will likely involve sending supplies and helping other survivors of the People of the White Egg. This seems quite obvious, given that it’s her primary goal of joining the Heroic Games in the first place. As part of going back and forth between Dagsion and Kunlun, she’ll also definitely have access to the Warp Gates in the various Grand Megaliths on the World Map.
## Orchel—Cat Priest
### The Crucial Thread That Fixes the Tapestry
Orchel is, by far, the game’s biggest elephant in the room. She may be the single most important character in tying the story's many plot holes together. We get little bits and pieces about her identity and how she’s essentially mechanical in how she interacts and fights. But more importantly, we know she’s wearing the mask to conceal the fact that she’s the spitting image of Yu Phas, or at least Credna told her to do so.
The many scenarios and interactions involving her don’t hide the fact that she may actually just be Yu Phas in a mechanical body. This is one of the many reasons her route will be essential, as Yu Phas is one of the most significant connections to the game's setting. She’s the sole reason the people of Damascar/Saramis came to be, and an even bigger connection to both the Dagdan pantheon and the other daughters of Balor, her sisters.
Aside from confirming that she essentially gets turned into soup in Dagda’s Cauldron, we’ll finally get an answer on how Credna managed to construct a robot that resembles and even shares Yu Phas’ personality, as well as how she interacted with her sisters. Plus, we never even had an interaction with Iliana and Orchel, especially given how distraught the former is when she gets unmasked during her fight against Creek and Nathan. There's also the matter of her unique Overblaze in Act 3, where she can forcibly activate her "Guardian Angel" mechanic, Elizabeth, which we're definitely going to hear more about from Credna.
Her route might give us answers about what happened to Solel at the end of Act 1, and maybe we might even see them meet if they decide to have her win the Heroic Games in her route. Her last few chapters may be the connection we need to see what actually happened in the months leading up to Iliana’s disappearance, Dagda’s resurrection, and, of course, Solel’s passing. Who knows? They might even just drop that Orchel already knows who Fortuna and Eshmel are when they expand on her route.
Gameplay-wise, her route will probably be the simplest. Given that there isn’t anything particularly special beyond her ties to the Temples, she’s probably the closest to a normal route players have experienced. Her way of building Renown will most likely revolve around tasks helping around Credna’s Temple, and maybe rebuilding Yu Phas’ Temple. She might also have something similar to Cai’s route where her sidequests revolve around Kindness and just making friends in general, as a big part of her character is that she tends to make friends with many of the characters in Dagsion.
## 2027 Can’t Come Soon Enough
### 200 More Hours to Come!
While all of these things are mostly speculation about the characters headlining the DLC, they do confirm one thing: there’s so much more to Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave that meets the eye. I’m not particularly ecstatic about replaying Part 1 four more times or paying for an expansion pass for content that was clearly about to be included in the game. But I am thankful that this DLC might give me the answers I have been itching for, since I really enjoyed piecing together the various details and plot threads the game was trying to weave.
Again, I could be totally wrong on these speculations, and part of that is because none of these things are confirmed. However, I could also just be right, and it’s fun to think about what might come in the upcoming DLC. Considering that Fire Emblem is a strategy game where you want to play percentages or defy the odds, it seems completely fitting that we can bank or gamble on something as simple as a possibility. But please, Intelligence Systems, give us a Master Class that uses Orniuses.
Sources: Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave Expansion Pass - Announcement Trailer - Nintendo Switch 2 Ask the Developer Vol. 23 – Chapter 1

item.title: Deadlock’s City Never Sleeps Heroes Review: The Good, The Bad, and The Cursed
item.description: 2026.10.26 Deadlock's City Never Sleeps update introduces six new heroes alongside sweeping changes to the game. We review the new heroes to see how they hold up against the rest of the cast so far.
item.content:encoded:
Deadlock's City Never Sleeps update introduces six new heroes alongside sweeping changes to the game. We review the new heroes to see how they hold up against the rest of the cast so far.
## Polls Are Closed, Verdict Is Out
For nearly three weeks, Deadlock players fought an election before every match as part of the City Never Sleeps update. More than 110 million votes were cast to decide which new hero would arrive next, and with Nurse Harrow's arrival, the polls are finally closed.
Now that the dust has settled and everyone has seen their abilities and playstyle. City Never Sleeps is Valve’s most creative batch yet, built around gimmicks like freehand painting, controllable chess pieces, and an unreasonable number of rats. With enough personal experience and data, I’ll assess how well each hero has held up in public matches and competitive play so far, and whether they will be staples or niche, forgotten picks.
### Rat King Gets Too Much Value From His Ultimate
There was never much doubt that Rat King would be released first, given his special relationship with the Deadlock community. A 2025 fan concept fueled mock leaks and "secret seventh hero" conspiracy theories long before Valve confirmed him, and the name had even appeared in Dota 2’s files among unreleased heroes years earlier. With his release, the monarch of New York’s Warrens now wants to establish Ratannia on Long Island, executing any humans who refuse to leave. Still, he’s considerably warm toward his own subjects, with multiple voicelines referencing more than 120 rats, including intimate details about a rat named Gumdrop and its whole polycule, as well as multiple lines featuring the fan-favorite Rabies Ronnie.
Rat King has the unfortunate balance problem of being too good and easy to play, which will always breed bitterness in competitive games. Scrap Grenade’s repeated detonations provide wave clear and long-range harassment, while Royal Pestments supplies a barrier that grows with his maximum health, incentivizing him to become a bulky bruiser. With Rat Swarm to shred bullet resistance, the monarch packs generous damage, durability, and utility into an easy-to-pick-up kit.
However, the biggest issue is his ultimate: Rule, Ratannia! His banner grants nearby allies movement speed, slow immunity, and damage reduction, while planting it damages and knocks up enemies and unleashes more rats. While Deadlock already has an area-denial ultimate with Graves’ Borrowed Decree, players can shoot the ghouls or heavy-melee the gravestone to break it; Rat King’s banner empowers the whole team, and there's no way to interact with it aside from leaving the area.
Even in uncoordinated pub games, Rat King’s banner is an easy-to-follow instruction: a "we win now" button that should be available during objectives like pushing Guardians or contesting Rifts—an ultimate so good that it got Sinclair, a hero that copies ultimates, nerfed. Dota 2 players have relived their trauma from Wraith Pact, an item with similar effects that dominated the meta before it was completely removed.
His objective control and ease of use have firmly placed him among the most popular heroes, with external trackers showing him in 67-70% of games. The huge sample size also makes his ~55% win rate dangerously noteworthy. Even Deadlock’s grassroots pro scene, Deadlock Night Shift (DLNS), has seen Rat King as a contested early pick and ban. The hero needs his power redistributed from his ultimate to the rest of his kit, because when the nerf hammer inevitably comes down on that ability again, his current overtuned usefulness will go with it.
### Baba Makes Spirit Heroes Feel Powerless
Baba had one of the most dramatic opening weeks of any City Never Sleeps hero. Players narrowly voted the Central Park Pigeon Lady into second place, and Valve later revealed that her contest against Solomon came down to roughly 0.5% of the vote, the closest matchup of the entire event. On top of that, her early impressions were abysmal, as Baba’s win rate hovered around 44% on day one. However, once players began deciphering her kit, her win rate soared to around 56% within the first week. Fitting, since Baba is an unsolved New York mystery tied to a witch coven, yet she's been seen occupying the same Central Park bench for 50 years, feeding pigeons.
The secret to Baba’s strength is Threadsap, an ability that makes Spirit-focused characters feel as though their builds have been temporarily deleted. Baba guides a scraggly thread with her crosshair, then it bursts along its path, stealing Spirit from enemy heroes while she uses it to strengthen her own shots and abilities. As long as this remains the core of her kit, she'll be a strong counterpick against Spirit-heavy compositions, especially if Deadlock adds a proper draft mode—someone like Kassadin in League of Legends or, well, Anti-Mage in Dota 2.
While she excels at sapping Spirit, she’s also one of Deadlock's most flexible and disruptive heroes. Granny Long Legs completes the Baba Yaga reference by turning her park bench into a pair of spindly legs, granting mobility, a knockback kick, and a ground-pounding heavy melee that knocks the opposing team around. Baba’s Brew cycles between a protective barrier, an area silence, and a scalding burn that reduces Spirit resistance. Her ultimate, Feed the Birds, adds even more CC on top of this, challenging a slow, then an eventual hex.
However, the trade-off is that Baba doesn’t feel as intuitive or smooth to play as other heroes, with nearly every ability asking players to manage an extra state, timing, or unusual movement input. After her first round of nerfs, Baba saw a huge drop in player retention, with her pick rate falling to 25% despite a healthy win rate. In Deadlock Night Shift, coordinated teams would rather ban her immediately than risk a game against her, and DNLS #60 locked her out of play for all seven games.
### Solomon’s Grand Design Is Undone by Awkward Controls
Solomon might be Valve’s most sauced-up Deadlock character yet. Every part of him is committed to the chessmaster fantasy, from abilities named after individual pieces to Alekhine’s Gun, a floating chessboard that doubles as his weapon and ammunition counter. Depending on his magazine size, every reload rearranges its pieces into one of 25 recognizable positions from chess history and culture, including the Immortal Game, Deep Blue versus Kasparov, and even a 2024 GothamChess match. Reaching 32 rounds, Solomon sets up the Double Bongcloud, the deliberately absurd opening played by Magnus Carlsen and Hikaru Nakamura.
Fittingly, Solomon is best understood as a control mage who wants a bird’s-eye view of the battlefield, treating New York’s streets as one enormous chessboard. Setup Bishop draws damaging diagonals across lanes and objectives, Rook Battery rebounds from walls before splitting into additional lines, and his ultimate, Develop Queen, repeatedly marks straight paths with delayed damage and stuns.
Kingside Knight completes the strategist fantasy by granting an ally barrier and stamina before letting Solomon physically reposition them, or by promoting himself into the King for a defensive escape to do the same. Valve even includes the niche Magic Carpet in his default build, letting him gain height and get a much clearer view of the fight.
Unfortunately, Solomon falls apart when an opponent stops respecting the board and simply punches the man playing it. He begins with only two stamina and depends heavily on Kingside Knight for protection, making him a prime target for assassins like Calico and Drifter.
Additionally, once Solomon gets all his pieces out, it feels like wrestling with the controls, as all the individual pieces fight for the same contextual right-click. The chessmaster might fit better in isometric MOBAs like League of Legends or Dota 2, although the latter already has Earth Spirit sharing a theme of repositioning objects.
While there’s much to praise about Solomon’s design, his complexity may intimidate more players from trying him and discourage those who do, contributing to his low pick and win rate. Despite that, organized teams are far more interested in him, as he is one of the most contested picks in tournaments so far.
### Deadman Danny Does His Best Work You Don’t Care About KDA
Deadman Danny may be my personal favorite of the City Never Sleeps batch, although playing his launch version felt like volunteering for one of Fairfax Industries’ product tests. The reckless crash-test dummy debuted with an abysmal win rate of roughly 38%, prompting Valve to deliver an emergency patch that addressed his worst points. With better numbers, Danny has become one of the most popular heroes in Deadlock, alongside Rat King, even though that sub-50% win rate suggests players find him fun enough to overlook his weaknesses.
What makes Danny unique is that he is a flying hero who doesn’t use flight safety, unlike Pharah from Overwatch 2 and what feels like half the cast of Marvel Rivals. Chimera Mk1 builds heat until he must dive back into the fight, and missing that landing punishes him with damage, a self-stun, and a disabled jetpack. Almost everything Danny does hurts him in return: rocket-jumping TF2 Soldier style costs health, and his ultimate, Close the Deal, sacrifices a quarter of his maximum health to carry an enemy skyward like Guilty Gear’s Potemkin Buster before slamming them into the ground. On death, Danny explodes and deals damage around him, which suggests Valve expects it to happen often.
Still, his skill expression and mastery of his high-risk playstyle make Danny a rewarding specialist hero, but it’s hard to imagine him becoming a regular competitive staple. His dives are telegraphed, his weapon is janky, and competent players will punish someone who dives into their backline on low health. A dedicated Danny player may eventually turn him into a dangerous pocket pick, but most teams will prefer heroes that provide the same initiation without also trying to kill themselves in the process. He is my favorite of the batch not because he is the strongest, but because no other newcomer translates their personality into gameplay with quite this much reckless commitment.
### Violet’s Conventional Design Hides Deadlock’s Most Creative Kit
Violet became the batch's most controversial hero not because her design is bad, but because it is unusually conventional. In Deadlock, players have grown accustomed to far more unorthodox characters, like a grandma riding a possessed bench or a sentient ball of goo, and some vocal parts of the community argue her design fits better in Overwatch or League of Legends. Whatever you think of Violet’s appearance, it is hard to deny that her kit is among the batch’s most creative once she picks up her brush.
The highlight of her kit is that Living Ink can turn her next three bullets into steerable projectiles, but its alternate function allows her to draw physical structures directly into the environment. Players already use those brush strokes for mid-fight cover, sealing corridors, building walkways, creating high ground, and blocking Troopers, ziplines, Guardians, and Midbosses from attacking. Her bread-and-butter combo has players use Still Life to stun enemies, then wrap them in Living Ink to root them in place. Players discovered this tech within the first week, and more creative tactics are sure to follow.
Flow State extends that creativity by letting her paint slide routes for her entire team, while Still Life rewards Violet for completing enemy portraits with permanent stat bonuses. Other artist-themed characters in MOBAs like Hwei in League of Legends exist, but Violet can physically edit and paint over the Cursed Apple, directly rewarding a player’s freehand input. However, Abstract Landscape has become the least beloved part of her kit.
Its enormous ink ring blocks sight, empowers Violet’s team, and punishes anyone who tries to leave, which adds another oversized, set-and-forget teamfight ultimate whose opaque walls turn already-chaotic battles into visual soup. It’s strangely generic and lacks the hands-on expression found throughout the rest of her kit.
Overall, Violet has been the most sensibly balanced release of the update, with a near 50% win rate and a fairly popular pick rate both in pubs and in DLNS, dominating her debut in the tournament. Still once players started wising up to her tricks, there’s enough counterplay to make her fair to fight against. Enemies can break line of sight on her stun and destroy her walls, and higher-ranked lobbies generally end faster, so she has less time to rack up stacks with Still Life.
### Nurse Harrow Gives and Takes in Equal Measure
Nurse Harrow may have arrived last, but she had the most fanatical waiting room in the update. Valve revealed that 22,194 players voted exclusively for her, one particularly committed supporter cast exactly 1,000 votes, and Harrow voters had the highest win rate of any hero’s supporters. Before her release, the severe uniform, living medical bag, and "Be Not Afraid" imagery led many players to expect an outright evil asylum nurse. Harrow is more interesting than that, and it's just another example of how Deadlock has wild lore. As a respected pillar of the Marble Hill Possession Ward, she sincerely cares about curing people suffering from supernatural possession; she is simply strict, emotionally detached, and willing to use methods her patients may find horrifying.
Harrow’s kit centers on giving and taking away. Leech Therapy steals health and time from enemy buffs, then returns them as permanent regeneration and fire rate. Wretched Vapors gives an ally faster actions and a reprieve from damage, but the target receives more damage when it ends. However, the centerpiece is Lurking Terrors, which opens her bag and exposes everything she has extracted from her patients, damaging enemies and preventing them from using stamina or movement abilities while they look at Harrow, eventually terrifying them into fleeing. Its reach makes the nurse particularly oppressive around Rifts, Midboss, or just protecting her team from a dive.
Compared with supports like Kelvin, Ivy, Paige, Dynamo, and Rem, Harrow’s healing is more directly tied to her weapon. Healing Needles replaces her magazine with aimed syringes, rewards headshots on teammates with extra healing, and replenishes its charges by dealing damage, like Moira in Overwatch 2—or, as a deeper cut, like a Medic with a Crusader’s Crossbow from TF2, except it scales differently. As a result, her early builds let her boost her gun's effectiveness alongside other utility purchases, giving her unmatched, consistent single-target healing along with decent damage.
The cost of this specialization is that Harrow may be the most team-dependent hero in the batch. She starts with no health regeneration, carries a small, unimpressive weapon that’s inherently weaker because of its -40% crit bonus scaling, lacks conventional escape options, farms slowly, and loses 25% of her accumulated leech stacks whenever she dies. Despite this, Harrow needs to stay in the middle of the fight, or she won’t deal enough damage to accumulate heals. Her strong, sustained healing and clutch ultimate will see her become a competitive staple, which is already evident in her 100% contest rate during her debut in DLNS.
### Valve’s Biggest Ideas Are Starting to Crowd Each Other Out
City Never Sleeps ultimately feels less like six new heroes and more like a stress test for how much experimentation Deadlock can support at once. Each addition has a memorable hook, from Violet’s living paint to Solomon’s chess pieces, and even the most gimmicky mechanics make these heroes feel unlike anyone else on the roster.
However, that ambition has begun to outpace restraint. Too many abilities fill the screen with walls, summons, and persistent effects, while all ultimates (except Deadman Danny) reduce teamfights to controlling, or simply abandoning, one enormous area. The result is a batch that is exciting to learn but often exhausting to fight.
Valve shouldn’t sand away what makes these heroes strange; it simply needs to preserve that creativity while restoring visual clarity, meaningful counterplay, and more distinct purposes for their ultimates. Fortunately, it is still a playtest, no matter how polished it may look, and everything is subject to change based on feedback. City Never Sleeps may be loud, messy, and at times overstimulating, but like any other game with a steep learning curve, untangling that complexity is part of the fun. This update further makes Deadlock a game no competitive gamer should sleep on.

item.description: 2026.10.26 Blue Archive's Japanese service is changing publishers, moving from Yostar to Nexon in January 2027. Read on to learn more about the transfer announcement and other details.
item.content:encoded:
Blue Archive's Japanese service is changing publishers, moving from Yostar to Nexon in January 2027. Read on to learn more about the transfer announcement and other details.
## Blue Archive JP Switches Publisher From Yostar to Nexon, Earning Mixed Fan Reactions
### Official Statement Made During Blue Archive JP’s Latest Livestream
It was officially announced on the October 25th Blue Archive livestream that the game’s JP publisher is switching from Yostar to Nexon in January 2027. Maintenance for the switch is set for January, with the detailed schedule to be announced sometime this November. Nexon Games remains the developer, and there are no planned changes to how the game is made.
According to community summaries of the livestream, Nexon ended the contract at its request, as the full handover of publishing rights will take about three months, and previously announced offline events will continue as planned. The Chinese version, on the other hand, is reportedly staying with Yostar.
### Players Must Link and Transfer Their Accounts
Nexon says all account data, including Blue Gems, packages, and items, will carry over, but players need to meet some requirements. Accounts must be first linked to a Yostar ID and registered for the transfer before the maintenance starts, while guest accounts can't be moved. After the switch, players will log in with a Nexon account instead, and anyone whose existing Nexon account was made through X (Twitter) has to register again.
Each Nexon account can hold only one Blue Archive account, so players with several Yostar IDs will need separate accounts, and Nexon Points can't be used in the game. Personal details tied to a Yostar ID, such as name and address, won't be transferred, and Nexon's own terms and privacy policy will apply. The procedure page is expected in November.
Other services are affected too. The PC version and Yostar's charge center stay available only until the maintenance begins, with Nexon preparing a new PC environment and a web-based payment option. Serial codes should be used before then, and items will keep their expiry dates. After the switch, players will receive compensation, including 100 free recruitments, and announced collaborations, merchandise, and events, including the Blue Academy Fest on January 23 and 24, are still on the way.
### Japanese and Global Players Weigh In Their Worries
Reactions have been mixed, and many replies from Japanese players are those of concern. Part of the worries stem from Nexon's reputation among the community, as Nexon is focused on different marketing strategies vs. Yostar in other gacha titles, as discussed on Reddit. While Yostar is very fan-centric in promoting a game, Nexon is regarded by the gacha fans as having a heavier focus on microtransactions and monetization as leading factors. Some are hoping that the quality would not lessen or drop when going through the transition.
Though Nexon Games already serves as the core developer in JP, Yostar was widely credited with establishing Blue Archive’s media and promotional efforts and budget, especially in Japan. Fans pointed to merchandise, songs, ASMR, ads in Tokyo, the online shop, offline events, and the Blue Archive radio show, all headed by Yostar. Some players also noted that there are noticeable gaps in promotions and marketing elsewhere compared to Japan, such as fewer offline events and collaborations, less content outside the game, and past translation errors.
Several fans asked Nexon to reconsider, a few hoped Yostar would return, and some fear for the game's long-term future. Others argue the change matters less than it seems. Nexon already develops the game and publishes it everywhere outside Japan and China, so some expect just a few in-game changes, and global players describe Nexon's publishing as steady, with occasional freebies and responses to feedback. A few hope that with this, Nexon could eventually bring Japan-only extras to other regions, though that remains speculation for now.
At this time, more answers are due in November, when Nexon plans to share the maintenance schedule, the account transfer procedure, and an interview video with Blue Archive's executive producer and Yostar's CEO. Nexon confirms its commitment to updating the game's stories and features hasn't changed ahead of the sixth anniversary on February 4, 2027.

item.content:encoded:
Goddess of Victory: NIKKE celebrates their 4th Anniversary with a Stellar Blade collaboration, new NIKKEs to recruit, and fan events.
## NIKKE’s 4th Anniversary Introduces Stellar Blade Collab, New Characters, Free SSR
### Marian, Scarlet, and Rapunzel Are the 4th Anniversary Stars
As revealed in today’s livestream, Goddess of Victory: NIKKE’s 4th Anniversary celebration comes in with plenty of new content, such as a Stellar Blade music collaboration, three new characters to add to the roster, and in-person fan celebrations.
Launching on October 29th, the 4th Anniversary update introduces Marian: Queen and Scarlet: Goddeath as recruitable NIKKEs, while Rapunzel: Sanctuary is a free SSR claimable up to four times through participating in anniversary events. Various in-game rewards will be available, with Commanders (NIKKE players) earning up to 259 free recruitment attempts during the duration of the event, with 4th Anniversary NIKKE selection boxes. These special selection boxes include: ⚫︎ Rapunzel: Sanctuary ⚫︎ Chime ⚫︎ Rapunzel: Pure Grace ⚫︎ Snow White: Innocent Days
Four new costumes also make their way to the game, two of which are obtained through gacha; Marian: Queen gets a “Last Affection” wedding dress costume where she “has attained happiness with her one true love,” while Snow White: Heavy Arms receives a “Lacrimosa” costume. Battle Pass costumes, Neon_Vision and Nayuta_Vision are also available on the update’s launch.
Stellar Blade, another popular action-adventure game from SHIFT UP, makes its way to the NIKKE universe with its second collaboration in the form of a soundtrack collection. Players can enjoy 22 tracks in TRACING THE STARS x Stellar Blade, added into the game with minigame backgrounds, custom note skins, and the special character appearance.
### Plus a Main Story Expansion, Story Events, and a Visual Novel Adventure
The Main Story will receive an expansion, adding Main Chapters 49-50. As the full-scale 3rd Surface Recapture War is at hand, this finale chapter marks the end of the Underground Ark plotline while also setting down the foundation for a brand-new story about to unfold. Amidst that, players can also tune into the “MARIA-n” Story Event featuring Marian in an unfamiliar environment, taking steps towards discovering long hidden secrets.
Additionally, there will be a minigame called “Fading Affection,” a choice-driven text-based visual novel with branching storylines that gives players the chance to revisit memory fragments and discover unexplored endings of the past.
### Taking Over Time Square Again Alongside In-Person Fan Events
NIKKE players in New York and Los Angeles can also take part in the in-person festivities. Alongside the update launch, a special NIKKE billboard on One Times Square (1475 Broadway & 42nd St.) will be on display for the entire day of October 29th. Eager fans can see Marian in action, taking over the heart of NYC, and take pictures with her.
For those in the West Coast, NIKKE will be featured in Animate Los Angeles in a special partnership for a “dedicated anniversary experience” that will feature plenty of photo displays such as the 3D illusion wall art and NIKKE-themed store decorations. Exclusive merchandise will also be on sale, and those who would stick around for a while longer can participate in special community activities. The NIKKE x Animate LA collaboration will run from October 31st to November 14th.
### Spanish Language Support To Be Added
As part of NIKKE’s “growth around the globe,” the livestream also revealed that full Spanish text localization will be added to the game on October 29th.
“We are excited to welcome more Spanish-speaking players from the LATAM region with the addition of the much requested Spanish language support launching with the 4th Anniversary Update, and we will continue to do our best to deliver exciting content for all our players going forward,” said Hyongseok Yoo, VP of SHIFT UP and NIKKE’s Game Director, suggesting that with that initiative, more localizations may be in development.
Source: Goddess of Victory: NIKKE Press Release

item.title: Valor Mortis Review | The Horrors Are the Highlight of an Uneven Soulslike
item.description: 2026.10.26 Valor Mortis is a first-person Soulslike set in an alternate-history Europe ravaged by a mysterious plague during the Napoleonic Wars. Read our review to see what it did well, what it didn't, and our overall impressions of the game.
item.content:encoded:
Valor Mortis is a first-person Soulslike set in an alternate-history Europe ravaged by a mysterious plague during the Napoleonic Wars. Read our review to see what it did well, what it didn't, and our overall impressions of the game.
## Valor Mortis Review | The Horrors Are the Highlight of an Uneven Soulslike
Soulslikes are more common than ever, with developers continuing to put their own spin on a genre known for punishing combat and fragmented storytelling. Valor Mortis takes a particularly unusual approach, bringing the familiar Soulslike formula into first person. Its monstrous creatures and grim, plague-ridden atmosphere evoke Bloodborne, while its mix of melee weapons, firearms, and supernatural abilities brings Dishonored to mind. Set against an alternate-history version of Napoleonic Europe, it has the ingredients for a distinctive take on the genre.
Developed by One More Level, Valor Mortis follows a soldier fighting through ruined battlefields overrun by reanimated troops and grotesque abominations. Memory fragments and cryptic encounters hint at the catastrophe that has overtaken Napoleon's forces, leaving plenty of questions about the world and its inhabitants. Yet its defining feature is also its biggest challenge: translating demanding Soulslike combat into a first-person perspective.
The shift makes encounters feel more immediate, but it also changes how players read enemy movements, manage stamina, and find openings to attack. Valor Mortis has some interesting ideas, though its combat, exploration, and technical performance don't always live up to the standard its premise sets. The result is a distinctive but uneven Soulslike that doesn't consistently make the most of its first-person approach.
## An Intriguing Narrative That Falls Short
Valor Mortis has a relatively straightforward central narrative, giving William Dowsett a clear objective: end the Crimson Plague ravaging Europe at its source. The story has its share of twists and turns, but it rarely develops its premise into something particularly substantial. Certain details, such as why Napoleon's voice echoes in William's head, remain unexplained for an uncomfortably long stretch of the game, leaving some of its most intriguing questions hanging.
The memory pools scattered throughout the world offer fragmented visions of the past, showing the lives of those who fought and struggled to survive the catastrophe. Seeing these moments alongside the devastation left behind gives the setting a more personal dimension, making the consequences of the plague feel tangible. However, these vignettes often feel disconnected from William's central journey. They offer glimpses into the lives affected by the catastrophe, but the main story could have used them better to give the broader narrative more emotional weight.
Other details emerge through encounters with the few characters willing to offer information. Lucjan, who saves William after his defeat by the mutated General Lothaire, seems responsible for installing the Lanterns scattered throughout the world. He also seems to know more about William's resurrection and the catastrophe than he lets on, yet the story offers little explanation for his knowledge or motivations. His cryptic behavior hints at a larger role, but the ambiguity around him rarely becomes a particularly satisfying mystery.
The in-game journal is a more effective touch, with entries about enemies and locales written from William's perspective rather than presented as detached bestiary descriptions. These personal observations give the protagonist more character and make the grotesque inhabitants feel like more than obstacles to overcome. It's a small detail, but one that adds personality to the world and gives players another reason to pay attention to the creatures they encounter.
Ultimately, Valor Mortis has enough intrigue to keep its story moving, but its narrative ideas don't always receive the development they deserve. The memory pools add a human dimension to the devastation, and the journal gives William a welcome sense of personality, yet the main plot and its supporting characters feel comparatively underdeveloped. The result is a serviceable story with an intriguing setting that doesn't fully realize its potential.
## Combat Has Good Ideas, Could Be Better
Valor Mortis brings familiar Soulslike mechanics into a first-person perspective, with melee weapons, firearms, blocks, parries, and dodges forming the foundation of combat. Endurance governs stamina, limiting how often William can attack, dodge, and defend before needing a moment to recover. The perspective takes some adjustment, as judging distances and tracking enemy movements can be difficult when everything happens up close. Attacks, healing, and reloading also lock William into animations, so it's important to find the right opening before acting. These mechanics reward patience and careful timing, but the first-person perspective makes it harder to judge when it's safe to commit, especially with multiple enemies.
Beyond crowd encounters, tracking threats outside William's immediate field of view can also be difficult. The Risen Grenadier offers a good example of how the game balances this challenge with opportunities for strategic play. Shooting its explosive bag deals heavy damage and disables its grenade attacks, while setting it ablaze can trigger the same explosion at greater risk, given how hard the enemy hits. Weak points like these reward players for observing their opponents, though landing precise shots with a controller can be difficult without aim assist.
The game also encourages players to watch enemy behavior, but awareness can be unpredictable. Some foes are easy to bypass, while others spot William from a short distance. Sneaking in for executions can also be unreliable when enemies turn around just as he moves in, making stealth a harder-to-judge option.
Transmutations offer some room to experiment with combat, though my playstyle mostly revolved around Flame and conventional melee attacks. Abilities like Stasis can create openings for burst damage, while the grapple is mostly useful for traversal and reaching hidden loot, with little use in regular fights. Neither system fully compensates for the limited variety of regular enemies, as long stretches of exploration involve fighting the same undead soldiers and grotesque creatures. Bosses provide a welcome change of pace with more distinctive encounters, but can't entirely offset the repetition between them.
Progression follows a familiar structure, with Catalysts used for skill upgrades and Ambers providing passive bonuses. Weapon upgrades offer another way to strengthen William, with each level unlocking enhancements for that particular weapon. However, upgrade materials are limited, and spending them is permanent, making it harder to justify experimenting with other weapons once you've invested resources. Exploration feeds into this progression by rewarding players who search for hidden loot and shortcuts, but the lack of a map makes revisiting earlier areas reliant on remembering landmarks and retracing routes. New skills can open previously inaccessible paths, though backtracking often involves searching for missed upgrade materials.
Valor Mortis has a solid foundation, with familiar mechanics and weak-point targeting that reward careful play. However, the first-person perspective makes combat harder to manage when multiple enemies attack at once, and repetitive encounters and limited exploration leave stretches of the journey less engaging than its more distinctive boss fights. Its progression systems give players a reason to keep improving William, but they don't fully make up for the lack of variety. The result is a game with promising combat ideas that don't always come together into a consistently satisfying experience.
## Grotesque and Unnerving As It Should Be
Valor Mortis establishes a dark, dreary atmosphere that suits its plague-ridden version of Napoleonic Europe. The sound design helps sell the state of these ruined battlefields. Its enemy designs are particularly effective, from undead soldiers that lurch awkwardly toward you to horrifying amalgamations of reanimated flesh that barely resemble the people they once were. Their movements, weighty attacks, and lingering sense of duty give them a disturbing presence, making encounters feel unnerving even before combat begins.
The first-person perspective makes these horrors feel uncomfortably close, reinforcing the game's bleak atmosphere. Seeing these creatures up close isn't always pleasant, especially with body horror involved, but that discomfort shows how effectively the designs get under your skin.
## Plagued By Some Rough Edges
Valor Mortis has its share of technical hiccups on Xbox Series S. Frame rate dips occur in certain areas, particularly those with dense foliage, while the corpse-covered battlefields seem to run just fine. Textures can also appear noticeably low-resolution, as though they haven't fully loaded, and the game's aggressive anti-aliasing further affects image quality. Performance isn't the only concern, however.
Some issues are more disruptive than others. Dying while aiming can lock the camera after you respawn at a Lantern, and crouching and standing up against certain environmental objects can cause William to clip through geometry. The fall-damage threshold can also be unclear, making it difficult to judge which drops are safe. These problems vary in severity, but they can make an already demanding game feel more frustrating than it needs to be.
The most severe issue I encountered was a visual bug in the Valley of Ashes, shortly before returning to the arena where the first boss fight takes place. The glitch completely disrupted the game's visuals and text, alongside another rendering issue that persisted for a minute or two before resolving on its own. I couldn't reproduce the problem afterward, but its impact was hard to ignore.
Valor Mortis also crashed once while I was simply walking through the environment, abruptly interrupting an otherwise uneventful moment. The developers released a hotfix shortly after launch that addressed graphical issues affecting some Xbox players and fixed several common crashes. However, the rendering problems persisted on my Series S even after the update. While the quick response is welcome, the issues I encountered still undermine the experience and add unnecessary frustration to a game that already demands patience.
## Is Valor Mortis Worth It?
### A Little Unsteady, But Worth the Plunge
Valor Mortis is worth checking out for Soulslike fans looking for a change of pace. Shifting familiar mechanics to first-person makes facing its enemies unsettling, while exploring a plague-ravaged Napoleonic Europe gives the journey a distinct identity. Going headfirst into the fray is quite literal here, and learning to read enemy movements from this perspective offers a different kind of challenge. However, awkward encounters, repetitive regular enemies, and technical issues can make the experience more frustrating than it needs to be.
Despite these shortcomings, Valor Mortis is an easy recommendation for players intrigued by its premise and willing to work through its rough edges. The combat has a learning curve, but adapting to its first-person perspective can make encounters feel rewarding, while its grotesque creatures and bleak atmosphere give the journey a memorable identity. It's not the most polished Soulslike out there, but it offers a distinct experience that fans of the genre should consider.
