item.title: GTA 6 Triggers the Great Release Evacuation as Rivals Flee and a Few Park Beside It
item.description: 2026.10.26 Xbox, Spike Chunsoft and CI Games moved Fable, Danganronpa 2×2 and Lords of the Fallen II to dodge GTA 6. Nintendo, Atari and a few indies are launching near Rockstar’s November 19 giant anyway, and their reasons show how much the industry fears it.
item.content:encoded:
Xbox, Spike Chunsoft and CI Games moved Fable, Danganronpa 2×2 and Lords of the Fallen II to dodge GTA 6. Nintendo, Atari and a few indies are launching near Rockstar’s November 19 giant anyway, and their reasons show how much the industry fears it.
## GTA 6 Empties the Calendar as Nintendo, Barbie and Indies Move In
### GTA 6 Has Cleared Out the Holiday Release Calendar
Somewhere between Halloween and Black Friday, the video game industry has left a very large parking space open. Publishers that normally fight for the holiday spotlight have shifted their biggest games into October or pushed them into 2027, all to keep a safe distance from Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) on November 19.
GTA 6 is the next main entry in the crime series from Rockstar Games, a label of Take-Two Interactive, and the first since GTA 5 arrived in 2013. Its release date has already been moved twice; Rockstar first aimed for fall 2025, then named May 26, 2026, and on November 6, 2025, Rockstar posted on X that the game would arrive on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The studio said the added months would let it finish the game with “the level of polish you have come to expect.”
Rockstar has since committed to that date in public. Its June 24 press release opened pre-orders on June 25 for a single-player experience priced at $79.99 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Take-Two reaffirmed the November 19 launch in its August 7 earnings release, and CEO Strauss Zelnick told analysts on the call that the level of pre-orders was “unprecedented and astonishing,” according to Variety, though he did not share numbers. Every rival publisher has been reading the same calendar, and a few of them have said so out loud.
Read closely, the calendar follows a pattern. The games leaving are the ones that would ask the same players for the same console time and the same holiday budget as GTA 6. But a few companies have decided to park right beside it—the games staying have each found a lane that GTA 6 does not occupy, such as a different platform, a different price tier or a different kind of player. That pattern says more about who is brave and who is desperate than any single release date does.
### Fable and Danganronpa 2×2 Moved Out of GTA 6’s Way
Xbox made the most prominent retreat. On May 29, 2026, its official X account announced that Fable, Playground Games’ revival of the fantasy RPG series, was moving from this fall to February 2027. The statement listed Halo: Campaign Evolved, Gears of War: E-Day, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Control Resonant, Star Wars: Galactic Racer and GTA 6 as the crowd of games filling the year, and said the new date would give Fable “the dedicated moment it deserves.” Xbox framed the delay as a way to plan its holiday launches around that field.
Spike Chunsoft was candid about the delay of Danganronpa 2×2, the expanded remake of Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair. The publisher announced the slip from 2026 to early 2027, and the game is now dated for January 14, 2027 in North America and Europe. In an interview with Crunchyroll at Anime Expo, producer Shohei Sakakibara said the team wanted more development time. When the interviewer asked whether GTA 6 was behind the delay, series creator Kazutaka Kodaka laughed and answered, “I wouldn’t have time to make the game while playing GTA 6.” The team also cited the wish to avoid a clash with “a certain AAA/AAAA title” releasing soon.
CI Games made a similar move for Lords of the Fallen 2. On June 23, CEO Marek Tyminski announced on X that the soulslike sequel, previously planned for fall 2026, now targets the first quarter of 2027. He said the extra months would give the team more time to integrate, iterate and polish, and that the new window sits outside a “highly competitive holiday period.” He did not name GTA 6, but the shift also moves the game out of Rockstar’s blast radius.
The October calendar shows the same instinct at work. Final Fantasy Resonance arrives October 22, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 follows on October 23 and Phantom Blade Zero lands October 29, a run of heavyweights packed into the final weeks before Rockstar’s date. Publishers rarely explain their calendars, which makes the Xbox and Spike Chunsoft statements stand out and raises the matter of what makes GTA 6 worth rearranging a year of releases.
### GTA 6 Is Feared for Its Pull on Attention and Wallets
Analysts have been describing the “GTA problem” for years. In an earlier report by Christopher Dring of The Game Business, one studio boss called GTA 6 a “huge meteor” and said the company would nudge its own releases three weeks earlier or later to stay clear of the impact. NYU Stern professor Joost van Dreunen told GamesRadar+ that after GTA lands, “the whole industry goes quiet,” and DFC Intelligence CEO David Cole predicted it would “suck all the air out of the room,” meaning its launch would draw so much player attention and press coverage that other releases would struggle to be noticed.
Circana analyst Mat Piscatella told GamesRadar+ that the game will be “the gaming event of the decade” and said he would want to avoid that week if possible, which is advice that rivals appear to have taken. From the same report, Serkan Toto, CEO of the Japan-focused consultancy Kantan Games, judged that any blockbuster once planned for holiday 2026 was very likely not happening after Rockstar settled on its date.
Rockstar has also fed that attention directly. Its 26-minute Extended Look, a gameplay showcase, premiered as a timed Netflix exclusive on August 27, and viewers reported problems accessing the service as the stream began with the sheer volume of people trying to access it. There, it was revealed that the game will give players plenty to do, with upgraded/improved features. For instance, Rockstar North’s Rob Nelson told IGN that robberies make up a big part of what players do between story missions, and that some story sections require earning cash by boosting cars or holding up places.
The cost of playing GTA 6 adds to the pressure on rivals. Pre-orders suggest a huge audience, and some of those buyers will need a new console on top of a standard edition priced at $79.99. Piscatella has warned that console price increases could surprise the casual buyers who arrive for GTA. In a Bluesky thread on October 9, he posted Circana figures showing US Xbox hardware units at an all-time low and PlayStation units at their lowest since 2013 for the year through August, with average console prices at record highs. “Price sensitivity is becoming a real problem,” he wrote. For a rival publisher, that means a shrinking pool of console owners and an $80 release competing for the spending of those who remain.
A few companies have decided to park right beside GTA 6 anyway, and the most conspicuous decision belongs to a company that read the same calendar and chose a date inside it.
### Nintendo Dated the Ocarina of Time Remake Two Weeks Before GTA 6
However, GTA 6 is not the only AAA game set to debut in November. Nintendo has dated The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 on November 5, 2026, exactly two weeks before GTA 6. The company revealed the date during the Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct on September 8, where series producer Eiji Aonuma showed the first gameplay. The remake, first announced in a June 9 Direct, reimagines the 1998 Nintendo 64 game for Switch 2, lets players hum or play ocarina melodies into the console’s built-in microphone, and ships its first physical print run with textured foil cover art. Nintendo’s presentation centers the release on the series’ 40th anniversary, with a 40th Anniversary Edition Switch 2 console arriving October 29.
Aakash Gupta, a product growth expert who previously worked as a Fortnite producer at Epic Games, wrote on X that “Nintendo didn’t swerve” while the rest of the industry did. In his reading, GTA 6 does not run on Nintendo hardware, the audiences barely overlap, and a remake of a game with a Metacritic score of 99 gets two full weeks of attention before Rockstar’s launch. He called the November 5 and November 19 pairing gaming’s Barbenheimer and concluded that Nintendo holds the only fanbase loyal enough to make that bet.
The date has entered pop culture as well. On October 3, Saturday Night Live’s Weekend Update seated Marcello Hernández as GTA 6’s Jason Duval and Mikey Day in a Link costume at the same desk, and former Nintendo marketing leads Kit Ellis and Krysta Yang discussed the segment in a video on their YouTube channel. They said Nintendo would likely have taken it as a compliment, since it presents Ocarina of Time as a worthy companion to the year’s biggest game.
Other companies sharing the neighborhood have turned the proximity into a joke.
### Barbie Rewind and Winx Club Give GTA 6 Its Barbenheimer
In July 2023, Barbie and Oppenheimer opened on the same day, and the bright comedy and the somber historical drama fed each other’s hype under the nickname Barbenheimer, which became the film industry’s best-known example of counterprogramming. Video games now have a version of their own.
Atari and Digital Eclipse announced Barbie Rewind in June, a compilation of 16 classic Barbie games from 1991 to 2007 wrapped around a DreamHouse decorating mode, and dated it for November 12, one week before GTA 6. The collection includes Barbie: Vacation Adventure, a never-before-released game, and it is listed on the PlayStation Store and the Xbox Store as well as Switch. GameSpot ran the headline “GTA 6 Gets Its Barbenheimer” and called the timing hilarious counterprogramming, noting that Atari also releases a remastered Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee on November 3. The Sixth Axis folded the two Atari releases into a nickname of its own, “Barbzilla.”
Winx Club: Moonlight Quest adds a second pastel-colored entry to the same month. Balio Studio is developing the open-world adventure in partnership with Rainbow, the company behind the animated series, and players control Bloom with 24 playable characters and 32 mini-games on offer. The studio has promised a November 2026 launch on consoles and PC without naming a day. Until it announces one, the game’s exact distance from November 19 remains unknown.
The independent studios entering the same window have an argument of their own to make.
### Indie Studios Are Launching Directly on November 19
Whether it counts as brave or desperate depends on the studio, yet indie developers have become the most aggressive group on the calendar.
Fairy Mount Games, a studio founded in 2025 by Błażej Żywiczyński and Denis Comtesse, whose earlier credits include Frostpunk, This War of Mine and Ori and the Will of the Wisps, will release its debut, the cozy strategy game Flame, Forest & Flood, on PC on November 19. Żywiczyński told GamesIndustry.biz, “Why should we just give up the entire month of November?” He pitched the game as an experience players can share with family and friends, and he pointed to the economics: he said the game could reach roughly a 5x return at about 30,000 copies sold, while GTA 6 would need to sell to every PS5 and Xbox Series owner to reach the same multiple. Wccftech noted this comparison leaves out an eventual PC release and GTA’s likely online mode, and that GTA 6’s absence from Steam this November gives PC-focused games an opening.
Devolver Digital turned a long-running office joke into a release plan. Volvy’s Adventure: Reslimed, developed by Devolver’s partner studio Doinksoft, arrives on Steam on November 19 at $4.99, with 25% off for pre-orders, and Devolver’s press release invited buyers to purchase it or spend $100 on GTA 6 “like some sucker.” Doinksoft designer Britt Brady and Devolver co-founder Nigel Lowrie told Kotaku that Brady pitched the game well before GTA 6 entered the conversation and that Devolver staff had separately joked about releasing something on the same day. They acknowledged GTA 6 will own the spotlight and named “counter-programming” as the approach that may work in Volvy’s favor.
### The Games Staying Near GTA 6 Occupy Different Price Tiers and Platforms
With all that said, set the November lineup side by side and the logic of committing to a November release date becomes visible. GTA 6 asks $79.99 for the Standard Edition and $99.99 for the Ultimate Edition, and it is available only on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Ocarina of Time costs $59.99 digitally and lives on Nintendo Switch 2. Barbie Rewind’s standard edition lists at $29.99, and Volvy’s Adventure: Reslimed costs $4.99 on Steam, which makes the Ultimate Edition’s price roughly the cost of 20 copies of Volvy.
Two of those lanes have a public rationale on the record. Aakash Gupta’s case for Nintendo rests on platform and audience, since GTA 6 does not run on Nintendo hardware. Fairy Mount’s Żywiczyński pitched his game as a cozy experience for family and friends, and Wccftech noted that GTA 6’s absence from Steam this November leaves PC-focused games an opening. Devolver named counter-programming as its approach for Volvy. Barbie Rewind shares PlayStation 5 with GTA 6, so it competes on price and audience, and Winx Club: Moonlight Quest leans on a fan base built by the animated series.
Applied to the calendar, that logic marks Nintendo’s move as calculated, the Barbie and Winx releases as counterprogramming and the indie launches as small-budget bets with a low break-even point. Each company is wagering that GTA 6’s buyers and its own are different people with different consoles and different budgets. If that wager holds, they can all share November with GTA 6.
### GTA 6’s Launch Date Reshapes the 2026 Game Awards Race
The calendar shuffle carries consequences beyond sales. The Game Awards’ FAQ, as relayed in our coverage, requires a title to be commercially available by Friday, November 20, at 9 PM PT to qualify for the 2026 ceremony on December 10, so GTA 6 clears the cutoff by a single day. Viral posts claimed the show made room for Rockstar’s game, and our coverage notes that an X Community Note pointed out the cutoff mirrors earlier years, when it fell on November 21 in 2025 and November 22 in 2024.
The date splits the field in two. Fable, Danganronpa 2×2 and Lords of the Fallen 2 are dated for 2027, so they will sit out this year’s awards and enter next year’s race. The games that stayed remain eligible, with Ocarina of Time on November 5 and Barbie Rewind on November 12 sharing this year’s ballot with the game that arrives one day before the deadline. Nintendo’s date puts Ocarina of Time on shelves two weeks before Rockstar’s launch, and the games that fled will compete in a 2027 field that GTA 6 will not be part of.
Eligibility is only the first step. According to the FAQ, most nominees are chosen by an international jury of more than 100 media and influencer outlets, winners are decided by a vote split 90% jury and 10% fan votes, and publishers can provide review copies or pre-release access to help later entries meet balloting deadlines. Fans are split on what that means for GTA 6. Some predict it will dominate the show, and others argue it could win on hype before players put in enough hours to judge it fairly.
Rockstar’s production story gives that debate its backdrop. Bloomberg’s making-of feature, as summarized in our coverage, counts more than eight years of development on the game, including two delays. Jason Schreier’s follow-up video, covered in our report on the weapon wheel, describes Rockstar spending months, if not years, testing replacements for the GTA weapon wheel before keeping it for GTA 6.
One date has now sorted the release calendar and the awards calendar at once. The games that fled traded a crowded November for a 2027 start and a different awards field, and the games that stayed will learn within days of launch whether their audiences truly differ from GTA 6’s.
GTA 6 launches Thursday, November 19, 2026 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, priced at $79.99 for the Standard Edition and $99.99 for the Ultimate Edition. Pre-orders are open, and per Rockstar Support, digital preload begins November 12 and the physical version contains a download code inside the box in place of a disc. A PC release has not been announced.

item.content:encoded:
Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is the long-awaited expansion to Capcom’s fantasy open-world action RPG, in which players explore an abandoned kingdom in the cold north. Read our review to see what it did well, what it didn't do well, and if it's worth buying.
Dark Arisen DLC Guide and All Content
## Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen Review: There’s Beauty in Simplicity When You Know It Already Works
You know what’s funny? The fact that Dragon’s Dogma 2 is going through the exact same thing its predecessor did, even going so far as to have the exact same name for its expansion. Starting from a heavily criticized base game for its design and technical faults, to cult-classic RPG status, thanks to how much its expansion completely overhauled the game. You may think it’s a coincidence, but I call it fate. Like, you can’t ignore the fact that the game's narrative is about realizing it’s a cycle that repeats until a new Arisen finally breaks it (or preserves it). But I digress.
One thing’s for certain, though: the Dark Arisen expansion finally realizes what Dragon’s Dogma 2 was trying to push for all these years.
The DLC adds the content it desperately needed to bridge the gap between the lethargic midgame experience leading up to its brutal endgame with the Unmoored World, and then some. But it’s not just the expansion that’s doing the heavy lifting here. The many patches that Capcom released over the course of the year overhauled the game in a good way, resulting in a completely different experience from what it had since its release.
## A Completely New Region Hiding an Even Darker Secret
If you’ve played Dragon’s Dogma 2, then you’d be familiar with how most of its main missions go. Accessing the DLC is no different; you talk to Captain Brant to fill you in with the details happening around the kingdom of Vernworth. He overhears a rumor about another Arisen discovered in the far north of the kingdom, a treacherous, abandoned region called Norgan.
By all accounts, it feels like just another day for the Arisen. Just another baseless rumor that lacks credibility. But that all changes when you get a nightmarish premonition where the kingdom is engulfed in a sinister darkness. Buildings engulfed in blue flames, ghouls rising from the ground, and an ominous moon that seems like it's staring back at you. It becomes clear this isn’t just some rumor, so you journey north to investigate this long-lost kingdom, only to find there’s not much to see in this abandoned, freezing wasteland.
Shortly after arriving in Norgan, you find a small settlement that briefs you on the situation in the region. Absolutely no one has visited the area recently, and there isn’t anyone else besides the people in the settlement that call the region home. So now you’re chasing a ghost in a region where the elements, the beasts, and even the Viking-looking bandits are out to kill you. Not a great start if you ask me. All of these lead you to check out the nearest stronghold for answers, as the locals have reported seeing something lurking in its empty halls.
It’s here where the story immediately ramps up to eleven. You find yourself face-to-face with a dragon breaking out of the stronghold out of nowhere, and with nowhere left to run, you decide to fight it. But something’s amiss here; the dragon looks lifeless, with its eye sockets hollow, and it has an ominous glow around it. It all seems hopeless until a mysterious warrior comes in, telling you that this isn’t your fight and that you should leave immediately.
I think this is already an infinitely better setup than its base game. Sure, it’s not the most interesting way to do it, but the change of pace is quite refreshing. Especially given that Dragon’s Dogma’s narrative tends to go on huge tangents with its political drama. This time, the mystery surrounding this other Arisen, this undead dragon, and this cold, merciless frozen wasteland is what’s driving the story rather than its b-plots.
In other words, the storytelling is very direct. In the DLC, every quest leads up to the mystery of why there’s an undead dragon on the loose, why there’s another Arisen, and, most importantly, how you’re supposed to address the problem. They don’t waste time with you going from city to city to get a hint of where the Grigori is, only to ask you to solve their city’s troubles before you can actually go on your way to slay the red menace.
The ending of the DLC is also done rather well in both the DLC's main campaign and its short post-game story, keeping the same simple, easy-to-understand plot without overcomplicating things. It resolves all of its plot threads and even leaves a little bit open to interpretation in its post-game content about who the true villain is and how they came to be. It’s a perfectly serviceable narrative that does a really good job of enhancing the base game in the grand scheme of things, especially considering that you have access to the DLC as soon as you’re midway through the main campaign.
## Not Just the Dark Arisen’s Efforts
Before I talk about anything further, let me address the elephant in the room. Yes, it’s not actually the expansion that’s making the game ultimately better; it was the recent overhauls that they made to improve the game’s design and make everything a lot more convenient. While this does put a spotlight on whether I should rate the DLC based on the expansion's content, the reality is that everything feels better because of how much the base game improved.
There are some design choices in its improvements here that "betray" the game’s intentional open-world friction. This, of course, refers to the Eternal Ferrystone and how it trivializes much of the backtracking you have to do. For context, convenience, or the lack thereof, is a big part of Dragon’s Dogma’s design. Much of the exploration relies on its limited fast-travel options and emphasizes an exclusive, player-curated experience.
]
This created a unique gameplay loop that forced players to explore the game’s massive world and deal with the random moments that happen during their expeditions. This also meant that players would have to carefully consider where they place their own points of convenience with the Portcrystals (the game’s placeable fast-travel points) they find, as well as consider how they travel with a finite number of Ferrystones that they can bring and use.
However, this friction is forced, which obviously means it isn’t something everyone will enjoy. Doing the trek from Bakbattahl to the Volcanic Island isn’t exactly enjoyable, even for someone like me who’s played enough of the game to make 3 different save files. Granted, I can’t exactly say how much of this was already planned before the DLC was even conceived. After all, the first game added this same feature in its DLC, so it could be something that was already planned before all of this can even be argued.
In contrast to the Ferrystone conundrum, features like Hard Mode and the new "reset" feature to compensate for it are certainly welcome additions. These add to the game’s overall replayability, which already reinforces just how much it asks you to play even more times than you think is necessary. Overall, Dragon's Dogma 2 is a far cry from what it originally was two years ago. And it’s only gotten better since then, with various performance improvements, gameplay-related design upgrades, bug fixes, and more.
## Lost Rites, Found Power
One thing that many were worried about was the progression, as people would be overleveled to all hell before the DLC comes out. But those worries were alleviated when people found out the hard way that none of the base game’s equipment did any meaningful damage. Similar to how they did it in the first Dark Arisen, the expansion is more gear-driven than tied to your character’s level.
This means that even players with level 200 characters are on the same playing field as someone who immediately jumped into the DLC at level 40. This means progression is purely reflected in the gear you have, which has its own pros and cons we’ll discuss later. For now, let’s focus on the individual mechanics, starting with the new dungeons in the DLC, the Lost Rites Trials.
The Lost Rites Trials are new explorable dungeons throughout Vernworth that, when completed, grant players gear with strength relative to their location. Additionally, these dungeons give an item called Offering Flame, which is needed to fully unlock progression in Norgan (we’ll talk about this later!). From a new playthrough perspective, these dungeons enhance the base game’s exploration and progression, giving players more content to engage with as they journey through Vernworth.
Like their rewards, these dungeons vary in difficulty, mostly depending on where they’re located in the world. Additionally, these dungeons may impose certain conditions before you can even enter, such as requiring only two skills to be equipped, locking the player into certain Vocations, or even requiring that players be accompanied only by their Main Pawn.
In terms of design, these are fairly straightforward. As they’re just big caves with stronger enemy variants to fight, with some conditions involved. However, this linearity comes across as a bit disappointing, especially given that the bar to beat was BitterBlack Isle (BBI) in the previous game. The linearity of the dungeons doesn’t really add any flavor, making them just another landmark once everything is said and done. I will concede that some of these Lost Rites Trials are great for introducing completely new enemies to fight, but these are few and far between.
## Re-educating With Norgan’s Vocations
Let’s move on to the next progression mechanic introduced: the Obelisks of Benediction. Throughout Norgan, you will come across interactable Obelisks that are tied to specific Vocations or classes. After finding said Obelisk, you offer Discipline Points (DCP) to get a Vocation-specific upgrade. It could be in the form of a new ability and its improved form, raw stat upgrades tied to the Vocation’s strengths, or even higher drop rates for Vocation-specific equipment.
However, to fully appreciate these rewards, players must complete one of the aforementioned Lost Rites Trials to obtain an Offering Flame, which can be used to activate these monuments. It’s a very simple system: you pay a fine, you get stronger. It may not be the most glamorous side-progression system out there, but it gets the job done. More importantly, this encourages players to explore more. Instead of just rushing through the DLC, you’d be coerced to explore the nooks and crannies to find the Obelisk of the Vocation that you prefer.
Lastly, remember how I mentioned that each Obelisk has a new skill for each vocation? At the DLC’s post-game, revisiting these locations lets you challenge past Maisters who grant you new skills after you beat them. I can’t stress enough just how amazing some of these skills are, as they are definite game-changers in amplifying a Vocation to its fullest potential.
One example is the Warrior’s Blood Pact, which has become one of my favorites because it completely eliminates the Vocation's weakness of being the slowest among the rest. Activating the skill grants you a buff that allows you to stack an invisible gauge by dealing and taking enough damage.
At maximum charge, you can reactivate the skill, which not only restores your Stamina to full but also grants a buff that lets you forgo charging your attacks and skills, and deals more damage. This turns you into the ultimate berserker, swinging around a hunk of metal with reckless abandon without caring for timing or charging your hits. Sure, your HP will constantly drain when the buff is up, but that is a price I’m willing to pay to kill my enemies three times faster.
## Relics Induce a Weird Progression Flow
All of these bring us to the actual meat of the DLC: how is the progression in the first place? For those who are unfamiliar with the series, it’s always been more of a gear-dependent RPG, where levels are the second-most important factor in your strength. But this is even more the case in the current iteration, as stat growths aren’t a thing anymore, so you could level without caring too much about which Vocation you’re using for the first 100 levels.
This is both a good and bad thing, and in the context of the DLC, it reinforces these in a big way.
The good news is that progression is pretty much tied to its content. You don’t have to worry about trivializing the expansion because you will never obtain gear in the base game that’s stronger than the gear in Norgan. So, any playthrough, regardless of how deep you are in the base game, is as fresh as starting at level 1. You’ll go through the same phase of seeing that your weapons are merely tickling the first few enemy mobs you encounter, scrounging every relic you find for appraisal.
Speaking of, the process of finding new gear is also quite easy. You get random relics from mobs or treasure chests, then ask someone in town to appraise them for you, hoping they're useful. It might be worrisome that the gear is randomized, but to be honest, they give out so much of it that it doesn’t even feel like a problem. You’ll almost always have a usable weapon or armor in no time, or better yet, just play on Warfarer so you can equip anything. Problem solved.
Enemy designs are also great in the DLC, with clear progression and distinct strength in their visual and gameplay design. From the simple direwolves and Beorcans to much bigger threats like the fire-breathing chicken wyvern Gagana and the Lesser Demons that roam the land, these new enemies provide a welcome challenge that makes you want to experience more of the already patented gameplay experience.
The bad news, however, is that going back to Vernworth will further diminish the base game’s difficulty. Keep in mind that the game recommends being at least level 40 to go to Norgan, which is definitely not close to the endgame at all. I get that you can circumvent this by playing the game in its new Hard Mode, but even then, having a full set of basic gear in the expansion is already endgame level for the base game.
This is where the DLC felt restricted in its design, as exploring Norgan had to be relegated to mid-game content because of the base game’s post-game in the Unmoored World. The result is a weird progression in both the mid-game and post-game, as the DLC spikes your power level to heights the base game can never match.
In the mid-game, you’ll move back and forth between the two regions to complete the Lost Rites Trials and explore Norgan. This becomes a problem—you become way too overpowered midway through the base game’s story because of the gear you need to actually survive the enemies around Norgan.
On the other hand, the post-game Lost Rites Trials do require stronger DLC gear, but they still run into the same problem of making the base game too easy. But the bigger problem is that you’ll move back into Norgan regardless, as the best weapons and armor are offered in defeating the post-game content in the DLC. Taken as a whole, this isn’t that big of a deal. The update did give you the Eternal Ferrystone, so you shouldn’t really have a problem moving back and forth. But it doesn’t make it any less weird.
## Is Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen Worth It?
### Absolutely! It’s Time to Book a Trip to Norgan
If there’s ever a time to get into Dragon’s Dogma 2, it's now. The improvements made to the game through its multiple updates and the DLC as a whole have immensely enhanced the overall experience, making it feel like the game that was promised back in 2024. I’d highly recommend this game for those looking for a fantasy action RPG that’s much more grounded in how it feels and plays.
While much of its additional content is rather simplistic, what was added was what it desperately needed to reinforce its overall gameplay loop. It’s still rather funny to think about the core theme of the series about breaking cycles, yet somehow, we get a case of history repeating itself with how the DLC basically repeats its own brand of success. Nevertheless, I’m all for it, and I’m glad I got to experience, or rather re-experience, this game in its best form.
## FAQ
### How Do I Access the Dark Arisen DLC in Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen?
The DLC can be accessed as soon as you unlock Vernworth in the main story. Talk to Captain Brandt to receive the quests for the Lost Rites Trials and the Dark Arisen DLC.
### Can I Still Access Norgan When I’m in the Unmoored World in Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen?
If you were able to receive the quest before entering the Unmoored World, then yes, you will still be able to access the new region. But if your current playthrough is in the Unmoored World without receiving the quest from Captain Brandt, then you will have to start a new game plus or use a completely new save to be able to travel to Norgan.

ONE PIECE: Grand Gourmet is a restaurant management simulation game by Kairosoft set in the world of One Piece. Learn more about the game’s plot, gameplay, release date, our first impressions, and more.
## It's a Surprisingly Addictive Time Sink Despite Failing to Keep It from Sinking
### Casual Fun Made for Fans
ONE PIECE: Grand Gourmet follows in the footsteps of action titles getting surprisingly cozy spin-offs, like Pokémon Pokopia and The Lord of the Rings’ Tales of the Shire. Kairosoft’s newest management sim places you at the helm of a floating restaurant alongside Luffy and the Straw Hat Crew in the studio’s signature pixel style.
Grand Gourmet is an incredibly fast-paced game that gives you an incredible amount of things to do. You’ll be in charge of everything, from naming the restaurant and developing a menu to designing interior and exterior spaces, developing relationships with customers, and even plating food. But a lengthy tutorial stage explains the function of each action so well that you’re never left confused. No knowledge of One Piece is needed to enjoy over 400 colorful sprites with unique animations and distinct, memorable personalities efficiently expressed through tiny bits of dialogue and quick interactions with the crew.
One Piece fans, on the other hand, will have their restaurant management experience elevated by their favorite characters in cute pixel form and references to the series. Right off the bat, the game starts off with a callback to the Baratie, a floating restaurant central to the series’ Baratie story arc. Along the way, each member of the crew that comes onboard introduces a new mechanic that directly references their talents and personality—you can come up with recipes alongside masterchef Sanji, buy supplies and get threatened with inflated interest rates by money-obsessed Nami, expand the ship with the help of shipwright Franky, and more.
There’s always a new customer request to fulfill, another town to explore for resources, a meal set to curate, a shop to build—there is never a dull moment aboard the Straw Hat Crew’s floating restaurant (I named mine The Grand Line). And yet, the $20 price tag—slightly higher than the studio’s usual, possibly due to licensing costs—feels just a little too steep. Minor flaws accumulate to create friction that ultimately takes away from an otherwise great experience and leaves the game feeling like it needed a few more minutes in the oven before release.
### Held Back by Bugs and Strange Design
My first nine hours with the game have been fun. Grand Gourmet gives me exactly the kind of high-stress rush I look for in any fast-paced management or cooking game. To top it off, the food and furniture look great, making it very rewarding to work hard for recipe ingredients or expensive flooring.
The game’s many mechanics fit together like puzzle pieces and directly influence each other. The resources you spend on one activity will reap rewards that can be used for another, which will in turn improve your game. Paying thousands of Berries for Luffy to explore a town might bankrupt you for a day, but it will net you ingredients and items you can use to buy things that will earn your restaurant more money than before. Although the game goes by fast and tasks quickly stack, you still have some control over your restaurant expansion as all tasks are optional and acquiring resources doesn’t require too much of a grind.
However, almost every great mechanic is held back by a frustrating bug, design choice, or UI feature. For instance, although decorating the restaurant is a lot of fun thanks to a great art style, Kairosoft’s signature control scheme that requires moving the environment to select an item was initially confusing. Even after I got used to it, it didn’t stop being annoying, as it felt like an outdated design that made simple tasks take longer than necessary. Limited furniture rotation due to the game’s fixed isometric perspective also restricts design options (some furniture can’t be rotated at all), and a lack of clear visual markers sometimes makes it hard to figure out if an item will be placed inside or outside of a wall.
While designing a lounge area using Luxurious Flooring, I hit a major bug that impacted my decorating experience. Typical of Kairosoft games, table design is attached to floor type. While this worked well with Deck flooring that gave tables an outdoor look, it completely stopped working with two other floor types and I was stuck with tables that didn’t match my floors. Because visual customization is half the game, this bug forced me to overhaul my entire layout and significantly impacted gameplay.
The lack of a furniture inventory, combined with the absence of a furniture sale system, makes for a frustrating experience: you’re forced to repurchase increasingly expensive items if you delete them, whether by accident or because they no longer fit your restaurant’s design and layout.
Outside of restaurant decorating, a few more flaws in the game’s design make it harder to play than it should be. Although turning off auto-advance for text is an option, the game ignores player preference and zips through tutorial text or character interactions, often too quickly. Lastly, while characteristic of Kairosoft titles, the oversized UI text crowds the buttons, giving the game an unfinished look.
All together, these flaws and strange design choices hold the game back from being a truly great casual time sink. Although more time with the game might prove otherwise, at the moment, Grand Gourmet is hard to recommend at full-price to someone who isn’t a die-hard One Piece or Kairosoft fan.

Chasing Kaleidorider is recruiting players for its next closed beta, the Doki Test, with sign-ups now open for mobile and PC. Read on to learn more about the test and other details.
## Chasing Kaleidorider Gets 2M Pre-Registrations Worldwide, Doki Test Sign-Ups Available
### Milestone Comes With Close Beta Applications and a Giveaway
Chasing Kaleidorider celebrates reaching 2 million global pre-registrations, and the team announced on its official X (Twitter) that Doki Test sign-ups opened on October 22. It's a closed beta with a limited player pool, and anything earned during the test, such as character progress and collected items, will be erased once it finishes instead of being kept for the full release.
Interested players can apply through a recruitment questionnaire, while regular pre-registration continues on the game's official website. The test's start and end dates haven't been revealed, so players will have to keep an eye on the official pages for updates.
The studio is also running a repost giveaway. Following the official @ChasingKaleidorider account and reposting the announcement enters players into a draw for ten $15 Amazon gift cards, with the giveaway running from October 22 to November 5. Fans have been signing up and hoping to be picked, while some asked what's new compared with the previous beta test.
### How to Apply and What to Expect
The Doki Test runs on iOS, Android, and PC. On the form, applicants can choose either Android or iOS as their mobile device, and those accepted into the mobile test also receive the PC version automatically, with progress synced across both devices. The test supports five languages for text (English, Japanese, Korean, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese), and voiceovers only cover Japanese or Chinese.
However, applying doesn't secure a spot, since the team is only accepting a limited number of players and will go through every application. Selected players will receive an email, and they'll need to sign in with the same email they used on the form. After the recruitment period closes, the official website will also add a page where applicants can look up whether they qualified.
Other standard beta rules also apply. Handing off, selling, or sharing test access or installation files is banned, and anyone caught will lose access, with violations possibly leading to legal action. Streaming, recording, and posting screenshots are allowed, but the studio says it will take action against leaks, such as data mining the client or spreading content that hasn't been released. Since the Doki Test is a work in progress, it is important for players to note that the visuals, text, voice work, and performance could look different in the final version of the product. item.title: Village in the Shade Review [First Impressions] | This Gorgeously Horrific Farming Sim is a Slow Burn Worth Enduring
item.description: 2026.10.23 Village in the Shade is a horror farming simulator developed and released by Nippon Ichi Software. Learn more about the game’s plot, gameplay, release date, our first impressions of the game, and more.
item.content:encoded:
Village in the Shade is a horror farming simulator developed and released by Nippon Ichi Software. Learn more about the game’s plot, gameplay, release date, our first impressions of the game, and more.
## This Gorgeously Horrific Farming Sim is a Slow Burn Worth Enduring
### Very Superstitious, Devil’s On His Way
Anyone who’s grown up outside of the city could tell you firsthand that the countryside, wherever you are, can be really weird sometimes. Livestock disappearing without a trace, the faint rustling of otherworldly creatures in the fields, hushed but urgent warnings on how to avoid offending the spirits that live amongst nature. It's unsettling, sure, but also deeply alluring. Village in the Shade seems to share that same, childlike fascination, taking the coziness of the farming sim genre to hide distinct, Japanese horrors under the soil.
Village in the Shade is a beautiful farming sim with an intriguing story and fantastic worldbuilding. It’s bound to excite virtual farmers that want a more macabre and uniquely Japanese take on the genre, and I was hooked even with its problems. It is gorgeously atmospheric in both the cozy daytime and the horrific nighttime, and getting to know its colorful cast of characters has been a treat so far.
Those problems are undeniable, though. The gameplay is mostly par for the course for the genre, though it does leverage its unique setting to its advantage. Its 60/40 split between farming and braving the horrors breaks up the pace fittingly well, even if I do wish it was more balanced and interconnected. The incredibly sluggish pacing, meanwhile, highlights the more predictable story beats and means that merely engaging with the game is a staggering commitment even relative to the genre.
Still, Village in the Shade does reward your patience. Like a hydrangea, it has a distinct beauty even when tilling the soil proves to be a chore. It starts off deeply gorgeous and alluring, which makes the snail’s pace of unlocking new abilities and story moments bearable before it gradually pays off. I do hope that, as the game progresses, it finds a more consistent rhythm and its momentum pays off into something amazing, but as it stands it's already worth digging into.
### Vibrant, Gorgeous Style that Mediates Horror and Coziness
The most striking thing about Village in the Shade, bar none, is its art style. The game is simply gorgeous, with that handcrafted, watercolor-meets-chibi-anime aesthetic working incredibly well for both the bright, wholesome side and the darker, macabre moments. The town comes alive in both daylight and the moonlight thanks to a vibrant color palette and a ton of wonderful little details for attentive players.
My favorite moments in Village in the Shade so far were just taking the environments in while fishing or tending to my farm. Watching the leaves fall to the ground and little birds and insects flutter around is constantly breathtaking, especially with how the game’s lighting works to give everything an understated, sunlit glow. Conversely, the way the screen seems to tear itself apart through the shaking effects and increasing fog of the night time horror portions gives Kagatsu’s hidden darkness an undeniable intensity.
The art style, ultimately, makes farming a rewarding exercise just by how beautiful you can make your farm look. The Japanese countryside feels a little more biodiverse than I expected, with Village in the Shade allowing farmers to plant everything from vegetables to trees to fields of flowers, and they all coalesce into nice, curated fields with minimal effort. The real highlight here, though, is how exploring Kagatsu at night with all of the yokai roaming around turns this once-cozy town into a tense, hostile arena to carefully navigate. Stealthily moving past pillars of eyes or giant monsters who abhor your very presence, with that same top down perspective and movement speed as you have while farming and strolling through the down, is nothing short of thrilling.
Even the character designs reflect just how effective the art style is at establishing the world and its atmosphere. Characters immediately communicate their character traits at a glance, whether it’s Kisuke’s brashness reflected in his sharp teeth and blond hair or Tobari’s cynicism being shown through their reserved pose and outfit. The yokai, meanwhile, are menacing without leaning into an exaggerated body horror that betrays the subdued, cartoonish style.
Some of these designs do end up blending together, though, while certain areas like the mines don’t feel nearly as distinctive in terms of their looks. Furthermore, the game’s tendency to start in Windowed Mode on PC makes the game look strange and compressed at first. Still, Village in the Shade is strikingly beautiful, and those aesthetics go a long way to making the game’s initial sluggishness palatable.
### Slower Growth than the Ginkgo Biloba Tree
Farming sims are, very consistently, time sinks. They take a while to get going, and reward players that really engage with the systems and put in the effort to make their plots beautiful. This should emphasize, then, just how long it takes for Village in the Shade to get going. The tutorial can take a few hours, while unlocking new abilities and items comes at a really slow pace. This is, ultimately, a double edged sword for Village in the Shade.
On one hand, this pacing forces players to soak in the gorgeous environments and the distinct personality of the area. Taking your time interacting with other villagers and finding secrets can be quite rewarding, even when your toolkit is fundamentally incomplete. At the very least, basic things like fishing, tilling, and planting are available after the tutorial.
On the other hand, though, as far as gameplay goes, Village in the Shade doesn’t exactly reinvent the wheel as far as farming mechanics go. Nothing in the game really necessitates these belabored tutorials, as farming and fishing work quite similarly to other games in the genre. Its more unique aspects, most notably the horror elements, will inevitably test your patience as it takes a while for them to even be interactive.
To its credit, the game regularly teases the horror elements through cryptic dialogue, notable story beats, and the odd jumpscare here and there. It establishes the atmosphere and looming dangers, but you won’t be exploring Kagatsu’s yokai-infested night time streets until at least 5 hours into the game, and that's if you go out of your way to skip through the farming portions. Exploring the town at night and learning more about the yokai and history of Kagatsu is alluring, especially as you unlock abilities and items that help your survivability, but more than 20 hours into the game and I just wish it was a more consistently engaging and interactive part of the experience.
Both halves of Village in the shade have their own merit, with the horror segments being tense, thrilling, and alluring to explore. The farming, meanwhile, is classically fun and engaging even with its simplicity, and players who just want to focus on that part of the experience can do so with the Village in the Sunshine mode that does away with the horror completely. I just wish that these two halves were better paced and balanced, and I’m hoping that as the game progresses the game finds a better rhythm.
### Classic Japanese Horror Makes for a Fascinating Double Life
Something that's always fascinated me about horror across cultures is how differently they approach the supernatural. Japanese horror and folklore seems to place a large emphasis on coexistence with spirits and monsters that exist not out of any malice, but as primordial forces of nature that one must respect. Village in the Shade directly implements the spiritual, rustic macabre of its world into both the moment-to-moment gameplay and the overall narrative, and it's all the more memorable because of it.
Village in the Shade follows Ame, a child who wakes up from a coma and stumbles onto Kagatsu Village. Kagatsu is a superstitious, distrustful village that maintains order through a number of strict rules; the most important one being that no one is allowed to venture into the town after 11PM. After offering their first harvest to the gods, Ame gains the villagers’ trust and begins a descent into the truth behind Kagatsu’s dark side. After Ame’s constant hauntings by Kagatsu’s horrors leads to their beloved pet chicken Pico dying, they’re led into a rabbit hole of breaking the sacred curfew and trying to survive against the town’s primordial spirits.
This inciting incident, even when it comes quite late into the story, is alluringly dark and sets the tone for the rest of the game. There’s already quite a bit of mystery even before Pico dies, such as Ame’s true identity, the time that’s passed since their coma, and what supernatural forces lie beneath Kagatsu’s sunny exterior. Having to stealthily explore the nocturnal, yokai-filled Kagatsu already carries such a heavy and layered risk, whether its risking your relationship with the townsfolk or gambling your health and inventory, and it makes that part of the game incredibly thrilling.
It makes it more interesting that Ame is, essentially, living a double life. By night, you’re foraging for clues and appeasing the spirits, praying that your mere presence doesn’t anger them; by morning, you’re helping the people of Kagatsu. You assimilate and become part of their community, you help them with their errands, and you learn more about them as people. In both cases, you’re an invasive outsider hunting for truth and identity amidst the mysteries of the village, and it’s such a cool narrative premise even in its glacial pace.
The characters of Village in the Shade are incredibly compelling in their arcs, whether its Yoh learning to deal with grief and accountability at such a young age or Hasumi’s insecurity with not being a "real doctor." They’re not all lovable, some of them like the stock broker Konno and de facto town leader Rin can be real assholes, but getting to form bonds with them has been one of my favorite parts of the experience.
Village in the Shade has been quite a memorable game, with its art style, strong writing, and fascinating premise carrying what’s otherwise a pretty standard farming sim. I can’t wait to dive back in and see if the game finally hits its stride pacing-wise. That premise is, ultimately, what I love most about it; the idea of a farming sim where you're an unwelcome anomaly that threatens the very fabric of the soil is such a brilliant subversion of genre tropes. Rules and consequences be damned, I need to know what happens next.

item.title: [INTERVIEW] STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT Devs Tease “We’re Pouring Our Hearts" Into the Series' Next Game
item.description: 2026.10.23 STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT developers discuss how 17 years shaped the remake, the new Moeka route, and their work with Chiyomaru Shikura on the next title. Read the full interview for more on what changed and what’s next for STEINS;GATE.
item.content:encoded:
“If there is one thing I can tell you, it is that the direction and descriptions in the game contain some kind of meaning. For now, I hope you will fully enjoy RE:BOOT and look forward to further updates in the future.”
STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT developers discuss how 17 years shaped the remake, the new Moeka route, and their work with Chiyomaru Shikura on the next title. Read the full interview for more on what changed and what’s next for STEINS;GATE.
## STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT Connects the Series’ Past and Future
### The Developers Are Already Working on the Next STEINS;GATE Game
We sat down with STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT producer Tatsuya Matsubara and scenario writer Naotaka Hayashi ahead of the critically acclaimed sci-fi visual novel’s console release on October 29, 2026, during which the developers confirmed that the series’ next title is being developed in collaboration with creator Chiyomaru Shikura.
"We are currently developing a new title in collaboration with the original creator, Chiyomaru Shikura," Hayashi said, translated from Japanese. "We’re pouring our hearts into this new project as we speak."
Matsubara added that the team is having "daily discussions" as they prepare to move forward with the next entry in the series. The developers did not reveal the title, release date, platforms, or story details.
The project itself dates back to 2020, when MAGES. mentioned in a business strategy presentation an unnamed title that is currently referred to by fans as "STEINS;???." The title was described as part of the team’s Science Adventure series. Shikura described its relationship with STEINS;GATE as similar to the connection between CHAOS;CHILD and CHAOS;HEAD. The game was presented as an independent title with STEINS;GATE characters appearing in its story.
Very little was revealed about the project after that announcement. Matsubara said in an interview with CBR that the team was still putting its concepts together for the game, with his role involving the translation of those concepts into the scenario.
We asked for an update on whether the new title is connected to a particular scene near the end of RE:BOOT. Matsubara declined to confirm or deny it.
"It is truly gratifying for a creator to know that their work is analyzed to such depths," Matsubara said. He explained that answering "YES" or "NO" would take away from players’ enjoyment and leave less room for speculation. He did offer one hint, though: "the direction and descriptions in the game contain some kind of meaning."
We will leave the scene itself unexplained here. RE:BOOT introduces new scenes and a new worldline, so discussing the details could spoil the experience for players who have yet to finish the remake.
### STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT Revisits a Classic With 17 Years Behind It
Seventeen years after the original STEINS;GATE, the developers had a much larger body of material to draw from when revisiting the story. Hayashi said the anime, STEINS;GATE ELITE, spin-offs, and collaborations had given the team "a much deeper understanding of the characters," which informed the remake.
That experience shaped some of the more practical changes in RE:BOOT. Modernizing the 2009 visual novel was one of the project’s key concepts, Matsubara said, with the team paying particular attention to pacing for modern players. Hayashi said they examined protagonist Okabe Rintaro’s "chuuni-style"* dialogue closely, since the original’s long tangents could make the early sections difficult to get through. The remake trims some of those exchanges and adds "TIPS" for internet slang that has since become outdated. *Chuuni: short for chuunibyō, literally “eighth-grader syndrome”, a term describing characters with outlandish mannerisms and delusions of grandeur
Still, the team wanted RE:BOOT to retain the character of the original. Hayashi said the developers kept its internet slang to preserve the atmosphere of 2009. According to Matsubara, they reached a similar decision on the email-based route system after considering whether they could simplify it. He felt that changing it could weaken the connection between Okabe and the player, since the mechanic is closely tied to experiencing the story through his perspective.
### A 2010 Drama CD Finds New Life in STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT
The remake gave the developers more freedom with material that had existed outside the original game. The clearest example is the new Moeka route. Hayashi said the team considered several ideas for an additional ending, including a joke harem ending, before settling on Moeka; fans had been asking for a Moeka ending since the original game was released.
The route draws from STEINS;GATE: Hyde of the Dark Dimension, a 2010 drama CD that Hayashi and Matsubara both worked on. Hayashi described it as a standalone "What if?" story. It was never expanded into another form of media, but he had wanted more people to experience it.
Bringing that story into RE:BOOT required more than adapting the drama CD, though. Hayashi said Hyde of the Dark Dimension had been designed as a self-contained scenario, so the new version had to be rebuilt around the main STEINS;GATE story. The writers needed to establish how the route could continue from the main narrative and how Okabe would ultimately decide to live with Moeka.
"We ended up making the story even harsher than the content of the drama CD," Hayashi remarked.
Matsubara, meanwhile, said he was glad that RE:BOOT could give Hyde of the Dark Dimension a wider audience after the drama CD remained known primarily to longtime fans. For Hayashi, revisiting the story fulfilled a desire he had held since its original release.
Seventeen years can change how a story is remembered. STEINS;GATE has grown far beyond its original release in that time, and RE:BOOT offers a chance to look back at where the series began with everything that came after it in mind and look forward to what’s to come.
For players who have yet to experience STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT, the remake arrives on PS5, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, and Xbox Series X|S on October 29, 2026. The game is already available on PC, and you can check out our review of that version below.
## Full Interview With Producer Tatsuya Matsubara and Scenario Writer Naotaka Hayashi
STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT is being played by longtime fans of STEINS;GATE and the Science Adventure series, but there are also likely players discovering the series for the first time through it. Did having both audiences in mind affect any of the decisions made during development?
Tatsuya Matsubara: Modernizing STEINS;GATE is one of the key concepts of this title, so naturally, we developed it with an emphasis on pacing for today’s players. At the same time, for core players, we thought that by rebuilding the presentation and other elements from scratch, we could create a version of STEINS;GATE they have never seen before.
Naotaka Hayashi: Even when the original version was released in 2009, there were already many people who found the characters’ heavy use of internet slang and "chuuni-style" dialogue difficult to get into . But now, in 2026, many of the words used in the game have become outdated, so I felt they would be especially difficult for younger players and people who haven’t played it before. So we based the text on ELITE, which puts more emphasis on pacing, and made further adjustments to make it as easy to read as possible, such as reducing Okabe’s "chuuni-style" dialogue and adding TIPS for outdated internet slang. At the same time, we also tried to preserve as much as possible of the atmosphere of 2009 so that people who experienced STEINS;GATE in the past wouldn’t be disappointed.
As STEINS;GATE was made in 2009, what did you find most difficult about deciding which parts of the original still worked for a modern audience?
Matsubara: The mechanic where the route branches based on email exchanges adds a layer of difficulty to STEINS;GATE, so we did struggle over simplifying it. STEINS;GATE places great importance on the sense of unity between Okabe and the player, and I felt that making the email-based branching easier would weaken the experience of seeing things from Okabe’s perspective. So we decided to leave it as it was in the original.
Hayashi: The thing I struggled with the most was whether to keep the internet slang. There are words used in the game that have become outdated and are completely incomprehensible to young people today, so I was concerned that when those words came up, they might interfere with the player’s immersion in the story. In the end, we decided to keep all of them and provide supplementary explanations through TIPS.
By the time RE:BOOT entered development, the original STEINS;GATE story had already existed as a visual novel (2009), an anime (2011), and a visual novel based on the anime (ELITE, 2018). How did having all of those versions available affect the development of the remake’s story?
Matsubara: One major advantage was that all of the developers were already very familiar with STEINS;GATE from the start. We didn’t need to give detailed instructions, which freed up resources and allowed us to spend more time refining the presentation.
Hayashi: RE:BOOT incorporates the best aspects of all the versions that came before it, so in a sense, it can be considered a definitive version. One of the biggest points is that we were able to update the characters. A great wealth of material has been accumulated through the anime, ELITE, and even other spin-offs and collaborations. Over these 17 years, both the cast and I have developed a much deeper understanding of the characters, and we were able to reflect that insight in the game.
How did you come to the decision to include the scenario with Moeka’s route in RE:BOOT? Was adapting an existing piece of STEINS;GATE lore always part of the plan, or did that direction emerge during development?
Hayashi: We considered some joke ideas, such as a so-called harem ending, but those were ultimately rejected. Early in development, we had already decided that the most appropriate content to branch off from the main story was a Moeka ending, which had also been requested by fans when the original version was released.
What did you want to accomplish with the new route that hadn’t been explored through the original drama CD, STEINS;GATE: Hyde of the Dark Dimension?
Hayashi: The drama CD STEINS;GATE: Hyde of the Dark Dimension was created as a standalone, self-contained "What if?" story. However, the story we added to STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT this time needed to be rebuilt so that it connects to the main narrative of STEINS;GATE and, like the endings involved the other heroines, becomes "a story that continues afterward." This is the result of making those adjustments. Also, after considering how to make Okabe resolve to live together with Moeka, we ended up making the story even harsher than the content of the drama CD.
Both of you were involved with the scenario for STEINS;GATE: Hyde of the Dark Dimension itself. What was it like returning to that story years later and developing it for RE:BOOT?
Matsubara: STEINS;GATE: Hyde of the Dark Dimension was a story known only to hardcore fans. I’m happy that this reboot will allow more people to discover its gritty world.
Hayashi: STEINS;GATE: Hyde of the Dark Dimension was released as a drama CD in 2010, but unlike the other drama CDs, it was the only one that had never been expanded into any other media. Because of that, I had always wanted more people to experience the story, so I’m especially happy that we were able to make that happen this time.
After working through the original visual novel and ELITE again, were there any scenes that you wanted to write differently for RE:BOOT? Is there a scene in the remake you are especially happy you got the chance to revisit?
Hayashi: We have included locations that did not exist in the original version but were added from the anime onward, such as the rooftop of the building where the lab is located, the laundromat where Okabe talks with Kurisu, and the pedestrian bridge near Yanabayashi Shrine. I think adding these locations is a significant step in allowing players to experience the atmosphere of Akihabara as it was in 2009.
The original visual novel was released in 2009. ELITE was released almost a decade ago, in 2018. After working with STEINS;GATE for so long, did you remember any scenes differently when you returned to them for RE:BOOT?
Hayashi: Kurisu’s speech in the original version was much harsher than I remembered, and I was a little surprised by how merciless she was toward Okabe. We have updated her speech to be milder in that regard.
Was there a particular part of STEINS;GATE that you knew you wanted to change for the remake? If so, what was it?
Hayashi: The part we reviewed most closely was Okabe’s "chuuni-style" dialogue. There had been criticism since the original version was released in 2009 that the conversations often went off on tangents, and that the poor pacing in the early part made it difficult to keep reading. So we reduced those conversational tangents, significantly improved the pacing, and adjusted it to make it easier to read.
Matsubara-san mentioned in an interview back in 2025 that you’re developing RE:BOOT in parallel with another title. Obviously, it might be difficult to mention exactly what you’re currently working on, but without getting into spoilers, does that project have anything to do with a certain scene players can find at the end of RE:BOOT?
Matsubara: It is truly gratifying for a creator to know that their work is analyzed to such depths. However, if I were to clearly say "YES" or "NO" here, it would take away from everyone’s enjoyment and the room for speculation (laughing).
If there is one thing I can tell you, it is that the direction and descriptions in the game contain some kind of meaning. For now, I hope you will fully enjoy RE:BOOT and look forward to further updates in the future.
Where do you both personally want to take the series next? Is there a story you’ve wanted to write for a long time that you still haven’t had the chance to tell?
Matsubara: I can’t go into much detail yet, but we are having daily discussions and making preparations to move forward with plans for a new entry in the series.
Hayashi: We are currently developing a new title in collaboration with the original creator, Chiyomaru Shikura. We’re pouring our hearts into this new project as we speak.

Explore the industrialized metropolis of Silvernia in Silver Palace. Read on to learn about its release date, its target platforms, and its announcement history.
## Silver Palace Release Date and Time
### PC and Mobile Closed Beta Test Recruitment Now Open, Ends October 10, 2026
Recruitment is now open for the Dichotomy Retrace Technical Test, for PC, iOS, and Android users. The start date for the beta test has not been announced.
Interested players must be 18+, and can sign up by answering a survey form. As this is a confidential test, selected participants will have to sign a non-disclosure agreement.
### Release Date TBA
Silver Palace is currently in development for PC, Android, iOS, and PlayStation 5.
## Silver Palace Overview
Silver Palace is an action role-playing game developed by Silver Studio and published by Singapore-based studio Elementa. It was announced in May 2025, with a release date yet to be announced. Interested players, however, can pre-register on the game’s official website.
The game casts players as a Detective in the industrialized metropolis of Silvernia, where they are drawn into a labyrinth of mystery involving corporations, crime syndicates, royal factions, and cults—all vying for control of a resource known as Silverium.
Combat involves both up-close melee attacks and ranged weapons or skills. Players can also investigate crime scenes, piece together evidence to form hypotheses, interrogate or takedown opponents stealthily, and make use of various travel options, including a flying horse, grappling hooks, and elevation devices.
## Is Silver Palace on Xbox Game Pass?
No, Silver Palace has not been announced for Xbox Game Pass.
## Is Silver Palace on PS Plus?
No, Silver Palace has not been announced for PS Plus.
## Is Silver Palace on Nintendo Switch Online?
No, Silver Palace has not been announced for Nintendo Switch Online.
## Announcement History
### 2026
Recruitment for the Dichotomy: Retrace Technical Test was announced through official channels. Sign-ups will be open until October 10, 2026.
Publisher Elementa debuted the House of Greed trailer during Gamescom 2026 Opening Night Live, showcasing playable demos, life-sized displays, and expanding the game's release lineup to include the PlayStation 5 alongside PC and mobile.
The schedule for the Silver Palace Monotype Beta Test was revealed in early January 2026. The test ran from January 13 through January 18.
### 2025
Recruitment for the Silver Palace [Monotype] Beta Test began in December 2025 and is scheduled to conclude on January 5, 2026. The official commencement date for the test remains unannounced.
### May 12, 2025 | First Announcement
Publisher Elementa and developer Silver Studio announced Silver Palace with an announcement trailer and a 10-minute gameplay showcase. Pre-registrations for the game also went live then.
